title: Magistrate seeks contempt charges against IGP | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 22 October 2026 00:30
-     - 100

IGP Priyantha Weerasooriya

Gampaha Magistrate Bandula Gunarathna yesterday directed the Court Registrar to forward case files concerning Inspector General of Police (IGP) Priyantha Weerasooriya to the President of the Court of Appeal, to initiate contempt of court proceedings over the alleged failure to comply with court orders.

Gunarathna expressed serious concern that the Police had failed to implement a directive requiring the IGP to issue a circular to all police officers against filing baseless cases against innocent members of the public.

The directive arose from a case involving a resident of Delowewa, Makandana. The Gampaha Anti-Corruption Unit had filed drug possession charges against under case numbers 1743 and 1744. Having found the charges baseless, the court ordered three police officers and the Police Department to pay the accused Rs. 200,000 in compensation. It also directed the IGP to issue a nationwide circular instructing officers not to institute frivolous cases against innocent people.

Despite being given sufficient time to comply, the Police Department had reportedly failed to issue the circular. Instead, lawyers for the Police Legal Division yesterday submitted guidelines issued on 19 October, 2026 by the Deputy Inspector General of Police in charge of the Western Province North. The guidelines applied only to the Gampaha, Kelaniya and Negombo police divisions.

Gunarathna criticised the Police for submitting instructions limited to a few divisions when the court had specifically ordered a circular covering the entire country. He observed that the move appeared to be an attempt to mislead the court.

Warning of the consequences of unwarranted arrests and baseless prosecutions, he questioned the sustainability of a system that encouraged the accumulation of cases instead of addressing the underlying causes of crime. He also expressed concern over the impact of such conduct on public confidence in law enforcement and the judiciary.

The case files forwarded include those concerning Weerasooriya’s alleged non-compliance, for the Court of Appeal President’s consideration of formal contempt of court proceedings.

title: Industry and construction lag personal credit | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 22 October 2026 00:28

Banks added Rs. 550 billion in Personal Loans and Advances in the first eight months of 2026, the most of any main sector. Credit to Industry grew by Rs. 347 billion and to Construction by Rs. 131 billion, and growth in both slowed sharply in May to August compared with a year earlier. The figures come from the Central Bank’s Monthly Survey of loans and advances by licensed commercial banks to key sectors.

Personal Loans and Advances rose by Rs. 49 billion in August, and their Rs. 550 billion increase for the year was growth of 24.8%, taking the total to Rs. 2.8 trillion. Growth has also picked up pace. In May to August 2026, credit in this category rose by Rs. 269 billion, 72% more than the Rs. 157 billion added in the same months of 2025.

Pawning drove much of that growth. It added Rs. 24 billion in August and Rs. 264 billion over the eight months, a 29.4% increase, to reach Rs. 1.2 trillion. It has grown every month this year, by between Rs. 22 billion and Rs. 50 billion a month. In May to August 2026, pawning grew by Rs. 123 billion, 52% more than in the same period of 2025. Consumer Durables grew by Rs. 56 billion, or 69%, in 2026 to Rs. 137 billion, but rose by less than Rs. 1 billion in August. Credit Cards grew by Rs. 20 billion, or 10.5%, to Rs. 214 billion.

Industry added Rs. 36 billion in August and Rs. 347 billion in 2026, growing 9.1% to Rs. 4.2 trillion. Its growth has slowed. In May to August 2026, Industry credit rose by Rs. 213 billion, 23% less than the Rs. 277 billion in the same months of 2025.

Construction accounts for much of that slowdown. Credit to the sub-sector grew by Rs. 20 billion in August and Rs. 131 billion, or 7.2%, in 2026, reaching Rs. 2 trillion. Its growth in May to August 2026 was Rs. 86 billion, 38% less than the Rs. 140 billion in the same period of 2025. Personal Housing including Purchasing/Construction/Repairs, which the survey counts under Construction, rose by Rs. 12 billion in August and Rs. 63 billion, or 7%, in 2026, to Rs. 966 billion.

Textiles and Apparel went into reverse. Credit to the sector fell by Rs. 23 billion, or 5.3%, in August to Rs. 406 billion. That wiped out the Rs. 22 billion it had gained over the previous seven months and left it Rs. 1 billion below its end-2025 level. In May to August 2026, its credit fell by Rs. 10 billion, compared with an increase of Rs. 50 billion in the same months of 2025. Other manufacturing sub-sectors kept growing. Food and Beverages added Rs. 13 billion in August and Rs. 49 billion, or 20%, in 2026, reaching Rs. 292 billion. Chemical, Petroleum, Pharmaceutical and Healthcare, and Rubber and Plastic Products added Rs. 46 billion, or 20.5%, to reach Rs. 273 billion. Fabricated Metal Products, Machinery and Transport Equipment grew by only Rs. 6 billion, or 2%, to Rs. 327 billion.

Services added Rs. 406 billion in 2026, growing 13% to Rs. 3.5 trillion. Only Rs. 14 billion of that came in August, the smallest monthly increase since January. Credit to Services grew by Rs. 244 billion in May to August 2026, 8% less than in the same period of 2025.

Financial and Business Services added the most within Services, growing by Rs. 196 billion, or 25%, in 2026 to Rs. 980 billion. Its credit rose in every month until June, then fell by Rs. 13 billion in July and Rs. 4 billion in August. Its growth in May to August 2026 was Rs. 74 billion, 41% less than in the same months of 2025.

Wholesale and Retail Trade had the largest increase of any sub-sector in August, at Rs. 27 billion. It grew by Rs. 106 billion, or 9.7%, in 2026 to Rs. 1.2 trillion. Its May-to-August growth was Rs. 112 billion, up 15% on a year earlier. Tourism grew by Rs. 27 billion over the eight months, then lost Rs. 13 billion in July and August combined, ending at Rs. 312 billion. Shipping, Aviation and Freight Forwarding fell by Rs. 5 billion, or 9.5%, in August to Rs. 46 billion. Transport declined by Rs. 3 billion in 2026 to Rs. 81 billion.

Agriculture and Fishing added Rs. 20 billion in August and Rs. 130 billion, or 14.1%, in 2026, reaching Rs. 1 trillion. Its growth has picked up. Credit to the sector rose by Rs. 74 billion in May to August 2026, 48% more than in the same months of 2025. Paddy rose by Rs. 25 billion, or 33.3%, in 2026 to Rs. 100 billion. Livestock and Dairy Farming grew by Rs. 18 billion to Rs. 93 billion, and Tea by Rs. 17 billion to Rs. 211 billion.

These trends have changed the make-up of private sector credit. Since end-2025, the share of Personal Loans and Advances has risen to 24.1% from 22.1%, and Pawning’s share to 10.1% from 8.9%. Industry’s share has fallen to 36.3% from 38%, and Construction’s to 17% from 18.1%. Services eased to 30.5% from 30.9%, and Agriculture and Fishing was unchanged at 9.1%.

The survey began in April 2025, and the Central Bank says it cannot be compared directly with the quarterly survey it replaced. August figures are provisional.

title: NDB posts 3Q PAT of Rs. 2.9 b | Daily FT

National Development Bank PLC (NDB) yesterday said it posted a Profit After Tax (PAT) of Rs. 2.9 billion during the third quarter. Releasing its financial results for the nine months ended 30 September, the bank said it delivered a strong performance during the period, underpinned by the resilience of its core banking franchise, disciplined execution of its strategic priorities, and the strength of its business model, despite the challenges arising from the fraud incident identified in April 2026.

The bank said the final forensic report of the fraud incident identified by the bank confirmed that the final fraud amount was circa Rs. 13.64 billion, compared with circa Rs. 13.58 billion as announced via a Corporate Disclosure on June 26, 2026, following the release of the interim forensic report. The incremental fraud amount has been recognised in accordance with applicable Accounting Standards. The gross impact of the fraud applicable for the 9M ended September 30, 2026 is Rs. 2.6 billion, whilst the applicable amount for the 9M ended September 30, 2025 is Rs. 4.5 billion.

The bank reported an operating profit before taxes on financial services of Rs. 15.1 billion for 9M 2026, after recognising the gross financial impact of the fraud attributable to the period amounting to Rs. 2.6 billion, which related entirely to the quarter ended March 31, 2026. This compares with an operating profit before taxes on financial services of Rs. 10.1 billion for 9M 2025, which has been restated to reflect the applicable fraud impact of Rs. 4.5 billion recognised for that period.

Post-tax profit for 9M 2026 amounted to Rs. 7.7 billion, compared with a restated post-tax profit of Rs. 5.1 billion for 9M 2025, with the net financial impact of the fraud reflected in both periods. Excluding the impact of the fraud, post-tax profit for 9M 2026 would have been Rs. 9.1 billion, compared with Rs. 7.5 billion in the corresponding period of 2025. The bank recorded a post-tax profit of Rs. 2.9 billion in 3Q 2026, compared with Rs. 3.0 billion in 2Q 2026 and Rs. 1.8 billion in 1Q 2026. Excluding the fraud loss, 1Q 2026 post-tax profit would have been Rs. 3.2 billion.

The bank posted net banking revenue of Rs. 32.6 billion, representing a 14.8% increase over the comparative period, driven by the strength of its core banking operations. This performance is reported before taking into account any financial impact arising from the fraud incident.

Supporting this performance, total revenue increased by 10.6% YoY to Rs. 80.6 billion. Net interest income (NII) was Rs. 25.4 billion, with a marginal decline of 2.2% attributable to the prevailing low interest rate environment and the faster pace of deposit repricing. However, the downside of these factors was mitigated through prudent balance sheet management, disciplined pricing strategies, and effective asset and liability management. The resultant net interest margin (NIM) was 3.6%, compared with 4.1% for FY 2025.

Net fee and commission income also expanded by 14.1% to Rs. 6.6 billion, supporting the diversification and resilience of the bank’s revenue mix. Key drivers of net fee and commission income were credit and cards and related services. Other non-fund-based income, comprising gains from trading activities, financial assets measured at fair value through profit or loss, de-recognition of financial assets, and other operating income, amounted to Rs. 3.7 billion during 9M 2026 (9M 2025: Rs. 2.6 billion). Other operating income included foreign reserve revaluation gains of Rs. 953 million, up from Rs. 396.8 million in 9M 2025.

Impairment charges on loans and other investments declined by 48.4% year on year to Rs. 3.0 billion, primarily reflecting the bank’s continued focus on asset quality management, enhanced credit underwriting standards, closer monitoring of asset quality and stage migration trends, and strengthened recovery efforts. The impaired loans (Stage 3) to Total Loans Ratio – Net improved to 3.0% as at September 30, 2026 from 3.8% at end-2025, while Stage 3 provision coverage improved to 65.4% from 59.1%.

Total operating expenses for 9M 2026 amounted to Rs. 17.5 billion, including Rs. 2.6 billion recognised under other operating expenses in relation to the fraud. The comparative operating expenses for 9M 2025, inclusive of the fraud-related expense applicable to that period, were Rs. 18.3 billion.

The bank’s total assets grew by 5.3% to Rs. 975.4 billion as at September 30, 2026, after recognising the financial impact of the fraud, compared with a restated asset base of Rs. 926.1 billion as at December 31, 2025. On an unadjusted basis, total assets as at September 30, 2026 would have amounted to Rs. 986.5 billion, compared with Rs. 935.8 billion at end-2025.

Net loans increased to Rs. 599.7 billion from Rs. 593.6 billion as at December 31, 2025, in line with the bank’s loan growth aspirations for the year, while total deposits grew to Rs. 717.5 billion from Rs. 707.2 billion. The bank’s CASA ratio stood at 20.7% as at September 30, 2026, compared with 23.9% at end-2025, reflecting industry-wide pressure on low-cost deposits amid the evolving interest rate environment. Total equity attributable to shareholders amounted to Rs. 82.8 billion, while Group equity stood at Rs. 90.1 billion as at September 30, 2026.

The bank’s liquidity and capital position remained sound throughout the period under review. Liquidity Coverage Ratios (LCR) in rupee and all-currency terms stood at 199.0% and 161.8%, respectively, while the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) was 126.8%. All ratios remained comfortably above the regulatory minimum requirement of 100.0%.

The bank also maintained healthy solvency levels, with Common Equity Tier 1 (CET 1)/Tier I Capital and Total Capital Adequacy Ratios (CAR) of 9.5% and 14.8%, respectively, as at September 30, 2026, remaining above applicable regulatory requirements. The corresponding restated ratios as at December 31, 2025 were 11.3% and 14.8%, respectively.

All KPIs for 9M 2026 are presented after incorporating the financial impact of the fraud, with comparative figures similarly restated. Return on Average Equity (ROE) improved to 12.9% for 9M 2026, compared with a restated ROE of 7.5% for FY 2025. Pre-tax Return on Average Assets (ROA) was 2.2%, compared with a restated 1.4% for FY 2025.

Annualised Earnings per Share (EPS) increased to Rs. 24.23 from a restated Rs. 13.83 for FY 2025. At Group level, ROE and EPS stood at 11.8% and Rs. 23.90, respectively, compared with restated FY 2025 figures of 8.4% and Rs. 15.77. Net Asset Value (NAV) per share stood at Rs. 191.48 as at September 30, 2026, compared with a restated Rs. 187.36 as at December 31, 2025. Group NAV per share was Rs. 204.98, compared with a restated Rs. 201.31 at end-2025. The share price closed at Rs. 109.50 (FY 2025: Rs. 141.25).

Director/Chief Executive Officer Kelum Edirisinghe said: “Despite the extraordinary circumstances faced, the bank continues to demonstrate strength and resilience. Our 3Q 2026 performance reflects the disciplined execution of our strategy to recalibrate the balance sheet and pursue measured and sustainable growth in line with our strategic priorities. Ultimately, these results reaffirm the underlying strength and resilience of our franchise. I extend my sincere appreciation to our customers, staff, regulators, shareholders and other stakeholders for their continued trust and confidence in the bank.

With regard to the fraud identified in April 2026, the findings of the final forensic report are generally consistent with matters identified through the bank’s internal investigations. The bank continues to pursue all available avenues for recovery and appropriate legal and internal action, and to implement relevant controls, technology and governance enhancements, while keeping the CBSL updated on the measures being taken.

While the incident has undoubtedly tested the organisation, our collective response has reinforced the strength of our staff and our institution. The commitment, resilience and shared sense of purpose demonstrated across the bank have sharpened our focus on controls, governance and operational excellence. It has reaffirmed that the true strength of the franchise lies not only in how we perform, but also in how we come together, respond and emerge stronger from adversity.

Looking ahead, we remain optimistic about the bank’s prospects. Our sound capital and liquidity positions, resilient franchise, talented workforce, technological capabilities and continuously strengthening governance and operational frameworks provide a solid platform from which to pursue the next phase of our growth.

We will remain disciplined in managing risk, capital, liquidity and costs to support measured, responsible and sustainable growth, while deepening customer relationships and leveraging technology to further enhance customer experience and operating efficiency.

As opportunities emerge alongside Sri Lanka’s economic progress, we believe the bank is well positioned to support our customers, contribute to the country’s economic advancement and translate the underlying strength of our franchise into sustainable growth,” Edirisinghe said.

The Asian Development Bank (ADB) yesterday said it has approved $ 100 million

 in financing to support reforms and investments that will strengthen social protection, economic inclusion, and well-being and resilience among the poor and elderly in Sri Lanka.

 

The financing comprises a $50 million policy-based loan and a $50 million project loan.

The ‘Promoting Resilience and Opportunity for Inclusive Recovery Sector Development Program’ will help the Government of Sri Lanka expand livelihood and employment opportunities for low-income households, improve eldercare services, and boost the effectiveness and responsiveness of the country’s social protection system. 

“Sri Lanka’s economic recovery must translate into meaningful improvements in the lives and livelihoods of vulnerable people,” said ADB Country Director for Sri Lanka Shannon Cowlin. “This program will help expand economic opportunities for poor households, strengthen social care services for an aging population, and build a more inclusive, responsive, and resilient social protection system that supports long-term recovery and shared prosperity.” 

Despite Sri Lanka’s continued economic recovery, poverty and vulnerability to shocks remain high, particularly among women, the young, the elderly, persons with disabilities, and populations in rural and disadvantaged regions. The program will address these challenges through policy reforms, institutional strengthening, and investments in livelihoods and care services.

The program will support the implementation of the government’s National Empowerment Program, providing 30,000 households identified through the Aswesuma social registry across six districts, including women and youth, with livelihood grants, employment and business support, skills development and financial literacy training, and access to reliable markets.

The program will strengthen the policy and regulatory framework for eldercare services and establish five model elderly day care centers in poorer districts. The centers will provide integrated care and support services while serving as demonstration sites to test and refine eldercare models that can be scaled up nationwide.

The program will also strengthen social protection delivery by enhancing monitoring and evaluation systems, digital platforms, case management, and data governance. These investments will be complemented by measures to strengthen the system’s shock responsiveness, including institutional arrangements and coordination mechanisms to ensure timely and effective support during shocks related to the changing climate and other emergencies, the ADB said.

The net is tightening on tax evaders, with the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) and the Excise Department yesterday signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to strengthen cooperation in combating tax evasion, money laundering and related financial crimes.

The agreement establishes a joint mechanism for the two departments to share intelligence and conduct parallel investigations based on the information exchanged.

The move follows the Prevention of Money Laundering (Amendment) Act No. 16 of 2026. With effect from 4 August, 2026, the Act classifies offences relating to tax evasion under Section 189 of the Inland Revenue Act, and offences under the Excise Ordinance, as unlawful activities in the context of money laundering. This means the proceeds of such offences can be pursued under anti-money laundering law.

The MoU aims to expand audit operations targeting tax evasion, minimise illicit financial flows and streamline revenue collection procedures. It also seeks to make more effective use of State resources in meeting Government revenue targets.

Commissioner General of Inland Revenue Rukdevi Fernando and Commissioner General of Excise M.B.N.A. Pemaratne signed the agreement on behalf of their respective departments at the Ministry of Finance, under the patronage of Deputy Secretary to the Treasury A.N. Hapugala.

title: Graduate growth falls short of economy’s skill needs: IPS | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 22 October 2026 00:01
-     - 90

IPS Research Director Dr. Nisha Arunatilake -Pic by Ruwan Walpola

Sri Lanka has expanded tertiary education without a clear strategy. Growth has concentrated at first-degree level, while the technicians, associate professionals and postgraduates that a productivity-led economy needs remain in short supply, the Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) said.

IPS Research Director Dr. Nisha Arunatilake presented the findings at a roundtable on Tuesday (20), on the IPS flagship report, Sri Lanka State of the Economy 2026. The report’s theme is ‘Durable Growth: Advancing Human Capital for Inclusive Prosperity’.

According to census data, the share of tertiary-educated people rose from 4% in 2012 to 6.8% in 2024. Over the same period, the STEM share (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) rose from 27% in 2016 to 31% in 2023. Dr. Arunatilake said the headline numbers hide four structural weaknesses.

The first is speed. Sri Lanka, now an upper-middle-income country, compares poorly with both established upper-middle-income economies and lower-middle-income countries on tertiary enrolment. In the comparison group, it ranks above only Pakistan, and its progress has been slow. She said the sector, now expanding at about 1%, would need to grow at around 4% to reach the levels of upper-middle-income peers. “We are, at the end of the day, a small economy competing with these countries,” she said.

The second is composition. Most of the increase has come from first degrees. The economy also needs postgraduates and short-cycle tertiary graduates, who are trained for practical, technical roles.

This gap is clearest in the workforce itself. Under international occupational classifications, knowledge workers are professionals, managers, technicians and associate professionals. The International Labour Organisation says these roles ideally require tertiary education. Sri Lanka’s share of knowledge workers compares reasonably with other countries. However, only about one-third of them are tertiary educated. Among technicians and associate professionals, the share is below a quarter.

The third weakness is gender. Women account for 57% of the tertiary educated and 59% of first-degree holders. Dr. Arunatilake said this was not a straightforward gain for equality. Women graduates are highly selective in their choice of jobs and are concentrated in teaching. Few women work in other professional fields, while male professionals are spread more evenly across occupations. She said the pattern shows the shortage of knowledge workers is partly a labour market problem, not only an education problem.

The labour market already rewards the skills in short supply. Compared with workers educated only to secondary level, STEM graduates find jobs faster and earn higher wages than non-STEM graduates. Dr. Arunatilake said this premium is likely to widen as technology advances, with renewable energy, data science and biotechnology growing faster than other fields.

She said skilled workers drive long-term total factor productivity, which is output growth not explained by more labour or capital. They do this by using resources more precisely. Precision farming is one example: it adjusts water and fertiliser inputs to raise yields. Skilled workers also drive innovation and help firms adapt to economic shocks.

The IPS recommended better information on which types of tertiary graduates the economy needs, so that supply matches demand. It also called for faster expansion of the sector, and for job creation to retain graduates lost to brain drain.

Dr. Arunatilake said the response must address both sides of the market. Policymakers need to understand why male students are not entering tertiary education, and why women prefer teaching. Better social protection and working conditions could draw more women into other professions, she added.

title: Unemployment decline masks deeper labour market damage: IPS | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 22 October 2026 00:00
-     - 71

IPS Research Fellow 

Dr. Pulasthi Amarasinghe 

-Pic by Ruwan Walpola

Sri Lanka’s return to pre-crisis unemployment levels is a misleading measure of recovery, the Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) said. Economic stabilisation has not delivered a comparable recovery in well-paid, productive and stable jobs, it said.

IPS Research Fellow 

Dr. Pulasthi Amarasinghe presented the findings at a roundtable on Tuesday (20),on the IPS flagship report, Sri Lanka State of the Economy 2026. The report covers labour in two chapters: one on employment, wages and productivity, and one on informality and resilience.

The unemployment rate returned to its 2019 level of 4.4% in 2024. Over the same five years, however, labour force participation fell by about 5%, and the employment-to-population ratio fell by about 4.5%. The 2025 survey shows some recovery, but both remain well below 2019 levels. Real earnings of salaried workers were also lower in 2024 than in 2019.

Dr. Amarasinghe said workers had absorbed much of the economic crisis through lower real wages and the loss of purchasing power from inflation. Around 300,000 workers left the country in 2022, which he said signalled a lack of employment opportunities at home.

The productivity data points to a structural problem. Labour productivity can rise in two ways: through gains within sectors, or through workers moving into higher-output sectors. Between 2019 and 2024, productivity improved within sectors, but the employment mix shifted the wrong way. As a result, aggregate labour productivity fell by 0.5%.

“You may think this is a low number, but given that this is five years and we don’t see a positive change in labour productivity, that is quite detrimental to any sort of economic activity,” Dr. Amarasinghe said. Workers’ ability to move into more productive sectors was limited, he added.

The recovery has also been uneven across groups. Female labour force participation fell from 34.5% in 2019 to 29.8% in 2024. Youth unemployment remains at 22%, which a recent International Monetary Fund report ranked among the highest in Asia. The share of A-level or higher qualified workers in [occupation category] rose from 32.8% to 34.9%, which Dr. Amarasinghe said pointed to underemployment and skills mismatch.

He said skills policy must respond to actual vacancies, but warned that “training and skill development alone won’t be enough if the jobs simply aren’t there”.

Informality compounds the problem. In 2024, 66.5% of the employed, or about 5.3 million workers, were in informal work. Formal wage employees earned an average of Rs. 63,000 a month, compared with Rs. 35,000 for informal wage employees. Informal workers also have no access to employment-based protection.

Dr. Amarasinghe gave the example of the roughly two million agriculture and fisheries workers exposed to climate risks. After Cyclone Ditwah, agricultural compensation went to those owning farmland. A significant number of agricultural workers who farm rented land did not receive the same protection.

Barriers to formalisation go beyond enforcement. Of informal wage employees, 59% work in [establishments] with fewer than five regular workers, which limits their scope to grow. Ninety percent have no written contract. Compliance costs, weak demand and the volume of regulation add further obstacles.

The IPS set out three linked priorities. The first is better skills matching, through training, vacancy information and programs aligned with demand. The second is an enabling environment for formal employment, through more efficient regulation and simpler registration. The third is stronger income security, through real wage protection, social security for informal workers and affordable employment benefits.

Dr. Amarasinghe said the three depend on each other. Skills earn no return without vacancies. Firms struggle to grow without formal employment. Without income security, workers find it too risky to move between jobs. “We simply need productive jobs, better earnings and income protection to advance together,” he said.

title: FinTech Forum to connect fintechs, build trust and open doors abroad | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 22 October 2026 00:00
-     - 33

FinTech Forum Sri Lanka Chairman and LankaPay CEO Channa de Silva

The FinTech Forum Sri Lanka Chairman and LankaPay CEO Channa de Silva in this interview speaks of the origin, vision and progress of FinTech Forum as well as industry developments. A technology industry veteran with over 30 years of experience, de Silva also makes some suggestions on the way forward.

Q: What is your vision as Chairman of the FinTech Forum?

A: My vision is for the whole industry to collaborate and move in one direction. Sri Lanka’s financial sector is robust and among the most technologically adopted industries in the country, with banks, finance companies and FinTechs already connected through LankaPay on a single national network. But each stakeholder was working in isolation: Among banks, finance companies, fintechs, startups, technology providers and international card companies, there was no dialogue, or even with the Government.

Banks mainly served the corporate segment, with an estimated 80% of our population living in rural areas and were not reached by digital financial services. Fintechs had no direct licensing route to business and no way to take their grievances or suggestions to the regulator either.

Around 2022, several fintechs and LankaPay got together and agreed that we needed an industry association in which every stakeholder is an integral part and a stakeholder. That became the Forum, with three key objectives. The first is to bring everyone to one table for a healthy dialogue. The second is to provide fintechs legitimacy, working with the regulators and the Government towards a licensing regime, not to stifle fintechs but progressive regulation to keep people’s money safe. The third is to create opportunities by attracting foreign/local investment for startups to scale and helping Sri Lankan fintechs expand into other countries.

Q: How do you aim to raise and strengthen awareness of the Forum’s role within the country’s financial sector?

A: The rails are in place and everyone, including the fintechs, are now connected. The next phase is awareness of the Forum’s role. We want to bring the industry into a progressive discussion mode, especially with international players coming on board.

Our membership of the Asia Fintech Alliance (AFA) supports this. It conducts monthly meetings and quarterly general meetings, our members are invited to its events and offer fintechs the opportunity to travel to other member countries for events, share knowledge, network and opportunities to speak at regional events etc. It also holds the AFA Awards and encourages members to apply to be recognised regionally.

Q: What sets the Forum apart as the industry body for Sri Lanka’s fintech sector?

A: It brings every part of the ecosystem under one roof including banks, finance companies, fintechs, technology service providers and international card companies. Earlier attempts by private entities to set up associations did not achieve much. The Forum also provides fintechs a voice and a legitimate channel to lobby the Central Bank and the Government, which they did not have before.

Our standing has also been recognised internationally. The AFA, an umbrella body of fintech associations from 16 countries and headquartered in Taipei, accepts only one association per country. It evaluates the association’s capability, membership, constitution and governance, and it selected the FinTech Forum as the sole representative from Sri Lanka. We have been a member for nearly two years.

Q: How does the Forum convene key stakeholders, including banks, startups and regulators, to the same table?

A: We started by bringing fintechs and LankaPay to a discussion around one table, and we agreed banks, finance companies, fintechs, startups, technology providers and card companies all had to be part and parcel of the body. The Forum grants each of them a place to work together, raise issues and hold healthy debates, and enables fintechs, who are not currently licensed by the Central Bank, a legitimate route to the regulator. We also work closely with the Digital Economy Ministry to support Government initiatives.

Q: What have been the biggest challenges and successes in aligning the goals of traditional banks, agile startups and Government regulators? Have you seen progress?

A: Yes, we have seen good progress. About six or seven years ago, LankaPay took the initiative to let fintechs join the national financial network by connecting through a single licensed bank or finance company. Since then, Digital payments have grown exponentially, mainly after the COVID pandemic. LankaPay, the national payment network, carries approximately half of all the total digital transactions in the country, and the other half happens digitally within the same bank. LankaPay handled over 537 million digitally enabled transactions in 2025 via all its systems with the total transaction value exceeding Rs. 42 trillion.

Most of the growth was seen in the business-to-business segment. A huge part of the SME and retail segments remain elusive, and it is where fintechs have a significant role to play. On the Government side, we have worked with GovTech (formerly ICTA) and the Ministry of Digital Economy to set up GovPay. We are seeing traction in several areas, though overall adoption is still low.

The biggest challenge is that fintechs are still not licensed or directly regulated. Payment service provider (PSP) licenses have not been issued, therefore room for fintechs to operate is limited. Yet fintechs are the growth engine of the sector, because they can reach every corner and individual of the country. We are on the right track, but there is still a long way to go.

Q: You have witnessed Sri Lanka’s digital development from its infancy. How does the current digital shift compare to the mid-1990s?

A: I have been in the technology industry since 1995, when Lanka Internet, the first internet service provider, started. I was the main engineer there and the first webmaster. I set up the first commercial website in Sri Lanka and was responsible for the first dedicated internet connection into the country.

The technology was very primitive then. We knew there was potential, but we never understood how pervasive the internet would become in people’s lives. There were no smartphones at the time. Connecting to the Internet directly in 1995 was a big advantage, because we were one of the first countries in the region to do so. But three decades of war held back infrastructure development until it ended in 2009, as a result we are probably not where we should be by now.

Still, we have everything in place to move forward. All the banks are fully digital and connected with finance companies and fintechs. The next phase is growing the retail segment and bringing the Government ecosystem into the digital world. We are not too late, and it is a matter of working together to get there.

Q: As an industry veteran with experience at major multinationals such as Microsoft and IBM, what global fintech trends should Sri Lanka adopt to be competitive?

A: We must be careful and practical, because each country’s context is different. India according to World Bank reports had banking penetration of 35% in 2011 before introduction of Aadhaar and reached around 89% by 2025. Sri Lanka does not have a digital ID, yet banking penetration is already about 90%, bank account penetration is not our primary problem, but getting people to put money into their bank accounts is.

Mobile money is also a classic case. It took off in Kenya because people had little access to cash as banks and ATMs were few and far apart. In Sri Lanka, when the two telcos introduced it a decade ago, we never saw significant growth, because people already had easy access to cash via banks and ATMs. QR has also been very slow to adopt. After two decades of card presence, tap-and-go could potentially suit people more than scan-and-pay. The same goes for online police traffic fines, which only worked because we deliberately chose a low-tech design coupled with SMS and offline methods to successfully implement on the ground. My message in every forum is to look at our own context and adopt suitable technologies but not to simply follow the region.

A recent islandwide survey shows over 70% of households have at least one smartphone, but only 36% of smartphone users use digital banking channels. Bringing the remaining 64% online is our low-hanging fruit, but the solution must fit the context of our country, our people and our culture.

Q: How is the Forum building consumer trust in digital finance, particularly as scams and fraud become the biggest threat to that trust?

A: What we are really seeing is not necessarily cyberattacks but serious financial frauds and scams. Fraudsters exploit people’s psychological and emotional context, tricking them into sharing passwords and OTPs or even making fraudulent transfers. An offer of 40 or 45% interest on investments is a typical bait, and people jump at it without questioning who could offer such benefits. Phishing links also take people to bogus sites and end up in frauds. We found approximately 11 internet banking portals of major banks had been replicated by fraudsters. Customers log in to the lookalike site by clicking on a phishing link losing all their money. These scams are the biggest threat to the trust factor.

Social engineering is almost impossible to stop, but awareness matters. Together with the Central Bank and banks, LankaPay ran a national campaign about a year and a half ago to make people aware of how they could become victims and how to avoid it. The basics were the bank’s OTP and the ATM PIN should never be shared with others. It is really a balancing act, because if we scare people off, they will stop moving to digital. We want them to adopt digital but use it safely, but the messaging must be carefully crafted.

Q: Can you explain any of the Forum’s initiatives that encourage new approaches to data security and fraud prevention?

A: Working with the banking industry, the Central Bank and LankaPay, we introduced mobile number validation to counter OTP fraud. When someone registers a bank account on an app, we make an API call to the telcos to check if the mobile number on the device matches the number the bank holds. A fraudster normally uses a separate device, and the numbers generally do not match. Since we implemented it, frauds involving OTP sharing have dropped to near zero.

The industry is also putting in place a centralised fraud management system to monitor transactions in financial sector entities, look for anomalies and monitor suspicious activities, and raise alerts.

It is a bigger problem than the financial sector could handle alone. Banks have very little control over phishing links. We have to work with the telcos and the TRC to block those links and sites. The Government and law enforcement must also be involved, because even if a culprit is caught, the problem remains if the law cannot punish them. We work closely with the Central Bank and the Ministry of Digital Economy as no single entity or sector can do it alone.

Q: What more needs to be done to bring the Government fully into the digital economy?

A: We need to bring the Government fully into digital. One example is the recent National Single Window initiative led by the Treasury. Importers and exporters have to deal with multiple agencies to clear goods, and we have enabled digital payments to Customs, Inland Revenue, the Ports Authority, SLSI and the import and export control department, about eight agencies in all.

Many more agencies still need to come in, because there is no point in digitising Customs, Inland Revenue or SLPA in isolation if a trader still must visit other agencies in person. The financial sector will make payments secure, efficient and seamless, but that is not enough if most of the remaining process is still manual. Unless people can complete the whole process digitally from home, adoption will not grow significantly. We are working with the Ministry of Digital Economy to automate the rest of the Government’s processes to make the end-to-end journey seamless.

title: BASL calls for withdrawal of terror, organised crime Bills | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 22 October 2026 00:05
-     - 37

The Bar Association of Sri Lanka (BASL) yesterday called on the Government to withdraw the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill (PSTA) in its present form and the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill (OCB). It warned that the two Bills would confer extraordinary powers of arrest, detention and surveillance on the Executive and curtail judicial oversight.

Both Bills have been placed on the Order Paper of Parliament. The BASL said that individually and collectively they would weaken judicial oversight at the very stages when protecting individual liberty is most critical. It said they would also create criminal liability with far-reaching implications for freedom of association, expression and movement.

The BASL has filed a Special Determination Application before the Supreme Court under Article 121 of the Constitution, asking the Court to rule on whether provisions of the PSTA are consistent with the Constitution. It argues that the provisions adversely affect fundamental rights and are inconsistent with Article 4(d), read with Article 3, and with Articles 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 14A. These cover the freedoms of thought, speech, assembly, association and movement; protection against torture; equality before the law; safeguards against arbitrary arrest and detention; and the right of access to information. It also contends that the restrictions fail to satisfy the permissible limitations on fundamental rights under Article 15.

The association noted that the Court’s jurisdiction is confined to whether a Bill is inconsistent with the Constitution, not whether it is wise, necessary or fair as a matter of policy. That decision, it said, remains with the Government.

The BASL said it had participated in good faith in the consultative process to prepare the PSTA, which is intended to replace the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA). It nominated Saliya Pieris PC and Chanaka de Silva PC to the Committee appointed to review the PTA. However, it said the gazetted Bill departs significantly from the draft the Committee approved. According to the BASL’s nominees, these changes were neither referred back to the Committee nor brought to the attention of its Chairman or members before publication.

The BASL said each of the principal departures reduces judicial control at the point of arrest and detention, or enlarges executive power:

It added that one of its nominees had dissented during consultations on the definition of terrorism, administrative detention and the proscription of organisations. Neither the Committee’s report nor the dissent has been made public.

The BASL said it wrote to Minister of Justice and National Integration Harshana Nanayakkara on 8 October, 2026, setting out its concerns and requesting that the departures be rectified, including through amendments at the Committee Stage, when Parliament amends a Bill clause by clause. It said it had received no response from the Ministry to date.

On the OCB, the BASL said that while it recognises the need to address organised crime, there was no public consultation on the Bill and the BASL itself was neither consulted nor informed of its drafting. The composition of the body that prepared it has not been made public. The OCB is stated to give effect to the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organised Crime.

The BASL said the Bill classifies as “serious crimes” all offences punishable by four or more years’ imprisonment, along with about 50 offences in its First Schedule. These include copyright and trademark infringement, excise and forest offences, and gambling licensing offences. The Bill’s extraordinary powers apply where such an offence is committed by a member of an “organised criminal group”, defined as a structured group of three or more persons acting in concert for a financial or other material benefit. The group need not have formal roles, continuity of membership or a developed structure.

Under the Bill, a suspect may be held on a Detention Order issued by the Secretary to the Ministry in charge of the Police. A Magistrate is bound to give effect to the order, for up to two months at a time and up to one year in all, with bail available only from the High Court. The BASL said no court decides whether detention is necessary before the order is issued, and that the OCB in effect bypasses the judicial process.

To illustrate the Bill’s breadth, the BASL cited an amateur band of five performing popular songs in a restaurant without the permission of the songwriter or label owner. On a literal reading, it said, the band would be a structured group acting for financial benefit committing a listed copyright offence. Its members could be detained for up to a year and their instruments seized and forfeited.

The association also objected to provisions allowing courts to determine membership of an organised criminal group by considering factors such as style of dress, hand signs, language, tattoos, association with known members, attendance at physical or virtual meetings and visits to particular premises. It said the risk falls most heavily on youth and marginalised communities. The Bill could also encompass peaceful protests, trade union activity and civil society groups. This is because its First Schedule includes Penal Code offences such as obstructing a public servant, which may arise in the policing of protests.

The BASL said the Bill sets aside rules that make confessions to police inadmissible, allowing statements signed by an accused in police custody to be proved against them. It also requires company directors to prove on a balance of probabilities that an offence by the company was committed without their knowledge or that they exercised due diligence. Persons sentenced under the Bill would be ineligible for any early release scheme. These provisions, it said, erode the presumption of innocence.

The BASL said both Bills must be read against Sri Lanka’s experience with the PTA. The Act was introduced in 1979 as a temporary measure and has remained in force for more than four decades. The BASL said successive governments have applied it arbitrarily to detain people without trial and to silence political opponents, activists, journalists, students and members of the public.

It cited the case of Attorney-at-Law Hejaaz Hizbullah, who was arrested on 14 April, 2020 and held under the PTA for 22 months (662 days) before being released on bail in February 2022. He was held for about 18 months before being indicted, exceeding the PTA’s own 18-month maximum for detention orders. In ordering his release, the Court of Appeal observed that the law’s ‘draconian elements’ had been misused.

“A law that can be used reasonably can also be misused, and given Sri Lanka’s experience, the BASL cannot discount the likelihood that the same abuses will be repeated under new names. A democracy that equips its police and executive with such powers risks drifting towards a police state,” the BASL said.

The association called on the Government to:

1.Withdraw the PSTA in its present form and restore the safeguards in the Committee-approved draft, including through Committee Stage amendments if the Bill proceeds.

2.Publish the Committee’s report and the recorded dissent, and explain on what basis, and on whose instructions, the gazetted Bill departed from the approved draft.

3.Withdraw the OCB and subject any replacement to full public consultation, including with the BASL, confining its scope to organised crime in line with the UN Convention and keeping arrest, remand, detention and surveillance powers under effective judicial authorisation.

4.Repeal the PTA without delay.

The BASL said it will continue to advance its position before the Government, Parliament and the Supreme Court, and reserves its rights in respect of the OCB, including under Article 121.

The statement was signed by BASL President Rajeev Amarasuriya and Secretary Nalin De Silva.

title: Pakistani podcast Kaisay signs knowledge partnership MoU with Marga Institute | Daily FT

Marga Institute Executive Vice Chairman Amar Gunatilleke (seated, left) and Kaisay Founder and Host Raja Jawad signing the MoU

Kaisay with Raja Jawad, a Pakistani podcast and media platform, has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the Marga Institute, an independent Sri Lankan development research institute founded in 1972. Under the MoU, Marga will serve as knowledge partner for Kaisay’s Sri Lanka-focused work.

Raja Jawad, founder and host of Kaisay, and Marga Institute Executive Vice Chairman Amar Gunatilleke signed the MoU at the Marga Institute in Colombo, in the presence of staff from both organisations. The agreement provides a basis for sharing research and perspectives on social and development issues. Specific activities will be developed jointly.

“South Asia has more to gain when we listen to one another with curiosity and respect,” said Jawad. “Pakistan and Sri Lanka have different experiences, but many of the questions before us - livelihoods, education and opportunity - are shared. Kaisay South Asia aims to bring the people working on those questions into a wider conversation. Marga’s knowledge of Sri Lanka gives that conversation depth, and I hope this will help valuable ideas travel across our borders.”

Gunatilleke said: “Research is most useful when it reaches people and informs public discussion. We welcome the opportunity to share Sri Lankan perspectives with audiences in Pakistan and across the region, while learning from experiences elsewhere. The value of this understanding will lie in the conversations and learning we build together.”

Sri Lanka is the second country in Kaisay South Asia, after Bangladesh, where Kaisay earlier signed a separate MoU with Research and Policy Integration for Development (RAPID), a Dhaka-based policy research organisation. Each knowledge partnership is country-specific: RAPID’s role concerns Bangladesh and Marga’s concerns Sri Lanka. Kaisay plans to develop work in Nepal next. Those plans will be developed separately.

title: HRCSL calls for organised crime Bill to be withdrawn | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 22 October 2026 00:03
-     - 30

The Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka (HRCSL) has recommended that the Prevention of Organised Crime Bill be withdrawn and substantially revised. It said the proposed law is wholly incompatible with the fundamental rights chapter of the Constitution and with international human rights treaties to which Sri Lanka is a party.

The Commission made the recommendation in a letter to the Minister of Justice and National Integration on the Bill, which was published in the Gazette on 6 October, 2026. It described the Bill as potentially more draconian than the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) of 1979.

The Commission accepted that legislation to combat organised crime is needed, provided it fully complies with constitutional and international human rights obligations. However, after reviewing the Bill, it concluded that the draft fell short of both.

A central concern is evidence. The Bill would allow confessions made to police officers not below the rank of Assistant Superintendent of Police to be used as evidence against a person. The Commission said these provisions virtually replicate section 16 of the PTA. It recalled its earlier observations on that section: making confessions to police admissible tends to incentivise torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment of persons in custody.

The Commission also questioned the Bill’s detention powers. Police would be able to obtain a detention order from the Secretary to the Ministry of Public Security to detain a suspect ‘who is connected with or concerned in a serious crime’. The Commission expressed deep concern over the inordinate scope of ‘serious crime’, which clause 3 of the Bill defines to include a range of potentially non-serious offences. These include offences connected to forfeiture or penalty under any section of the Customs Ordinance and the import of animals without permits under the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance. They also include infringement of copyright, industrial designs, patents or marks under the Intellectual Property Act, No. 36 of 2003.

The Commission described the Bill’s test for membership of an organised criminal group as extremely broad. The factors include adopting the style of dress, hand signs, language or tattoos used by known members of such a group, and even mere association with known members. As a result, the Commission said, the Bill casts a wide and unreasonable net over Sri Lankan citizens.

The Commission further said the Bill, contrary to article 13(2) of the Constitution, strips the judiciary of its ordinary discretionary powers to decide whether a suspect should be discharged, released on bail or remanded. For example, the Bill compels a Magistrate to remand a suspect or give effect to a detention order. The Commission repeated the recommendation it made on the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill: a judicial officer must at all times have meaningful authority to discharge a suspect or grant bail.

title: Protecting Buddhism is a constitutional duty — but are we truly fostering the Buddha Sasana? | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 22 October 2026 00:26
-     - 57

Respect for the Sangha should never be confused with unquestioning acceptance of the conduct of every individual monk. Instances of intimidation, incitement, violence or other unlawful behaviour must be addressed according to the law, irrespective of the religious standing of those involved

Sri Lanka’s Buddhist civilisational heritage

Sri Lanka possesses an extraordinary Buddhist heritage extending over more than 2,300 years, forming part of a Buddhist tradition that spans approximately 2,500 years.

Since the introduction of Buddhism during the reign of King Devanampiya Tissa in the third century BCE, its influence has extended far beyond religious observance. Buddhism has profoundly shaped Sri Lanka’s literature, education, architecture, cultural traditions, moral values, social institutions and national identity.

The ancient cities of Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa, magnificent stupas, monasteries, Buddhist scholarship and enduring traditions of learning all bear testimony to this remarkable inheritance.

The ancient cities of Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa, their magnificent stupas, monasteries, Buddhist scholarship and enduring traditions of learning and sophisticated irrigation systems bear testimony to this remarkable civilisational inheritance. The enduring concept of “Wewa and Dagaba” (the irrigation tank and the Buddhist stupa) captures a distinctive feature of Sri Lanka’s historical development, where agriculture, community wellbeing and spiritual life were closely interconnected. The wewa sustained livelihoods and agricultural prosperity, while the dagaba symbolised the spiritual and ethical foundations of society. Together, they reflected a civilisation in which material wellbeing and spiritual development were regarded as complementary aspects of community life.

Protecting such a heritage is not merely a matter of religious preference. It is also about preserving an important foundation of Sri Lanka’s historical and cultural identity.

However, discussions surrounding Buddhism’s constitutional position frequently become entangled in political controversies, religious emotions and competing interpretations of national identity.

A more constructive discussion requires us to distinguish three interconnected responsibilities: protecting Buddhism’s historical and constitutional position, actively fostering the Buddha Sasana, and ensuring that those who profess to uphold Buddhism demonstrate its teachings through their conduct.

These responsibilities should complement rather than contradict one another.

Constitutional recognition of religion is not unique to Sri Lanka

Sri Lanka is certainly not alone in constitutionally recognising a religion that has historically shaped its civilisation. Several European countries, including established constitutional democracies, explicitly recognise Christianity or particular Christian denominations in their constitutions.

Denmark: Section 4 of the Danish Constitution recognises the Evangelical Lutheran Church as the established Church of Denmark and requires the State to support it.

Greece: Article 3 of the Greek Constitution recognises Eastern Orthodox Christianity as the prevailing religion, reflecting its longstanding association with Greek history, culture and national identity.

Iceland: Article 62 declares the Evangelical Lutheran Church to be the State Church and expressly provides that it shall be supported and protected by the State.

Malta: Article 2 declares the Roman Catholic Apostolic Religion to be the religion of Malta, reflecting the country’s historical religious identity.


Liechtenstein: Article 37 recognises the Roman Catholic Church as the national church, extending special constitutional protection while guaranteeing freedom of religion and conscience.

These constitutional arrangements are not identical. Some establish a State Church, while others recognise a prevailing or historically significant religion. The nature of government support and the legal relationship between religious institutions and the State also differ.

Nevertheless, they demonstrate an important principle: constitutional recognition of a historically influential religion is not inherently incompatible with democracy, modern constitutional governance or religious freedom. Such recognition does not automatically justify every religious privilege, nor does it remove the State’s responsibility to safeguard the rights of other religious communities. For Sri Lanka, therefore, the more meaningful question is not simply whether Buddhism deserves constitutional recognition, but how that recognition should be interpreted and translated into constructive national responsibilities.

Sri Lanka’s Article 9: A constitutional duty to protect and foster Buddhism

Article 9 of Sri Lanka’s Constitution states:

“The Republic of Sri Lanka shall give to Buddhism the foremost place and accordingly it shall be the duty of the State to protect and foster the Buddha Sasana, while assuring to all religions the rights granted by Articles 10 and 14(1)(e).”

The wording is particularly important because it establishes two distinct responsibilities: to protect Buddhism and to foster the Buddha Sasana.

Article 9 is not merely a symbolic acknowledgement of Buddhism’s historical contribution. It imposes an affirmative constitutional duty upon the State. At the same time, Sri Lanka’s Constitution protects freedom of thought, conscience and religion, while Article 12 guarantees equality before the law.

Consequently, recognising Buddhism’s foremost position should not be interpreted as authorising discrimination, religious intimidation or the denial of fundamental rights to other communities. Sri Lanka’s Hindu, Muslim, Christian and other religious communities have also contributed immensely to the country’s development. Their dignity, religious freedom and equal citizenship must remain protected. Recognising Buddhism’s special historical position and respecting the rights of all citizens need not be mutually exclusive responsibilities.

However, while considerable public attention has been directed towards protecting Buddhism’s constitutional position, the equally important obligation to foster the Buddha Sasana deserves greater national attention.

Protecting Buddhism and fostering Buddhism are not the same

Protecting Buddhism involves safeguarding its scriptures, religious institutions, monasteries, sacred sites, historical monuments, traditions and freedom of religious practice. 

Fostering Buddhism requires something deeper and more enduring. It involves strengthening understanding of the Dhamma, promoting observance of the Vinaya, improving Buddhist education, encouraging ethical behaviour and ensuring that Buddhist teachings continue to make a meaningful contribution to contemporary society.

Preserving temples, restoring historical monuments, sponsoring religious ceremonies and supporting religious institutions are undoubtedly worthwhile activities. 

However, such activities alone cannot establish that Buddhism is flourishing spiritually or ethically. We must also ask whether the Buddha’s teachings are genuinely understood, practised and transmitted to future generations.

Are Buddhist educational institutions adequately preparing young people to understand the Dhamma beyond rituals and ceremonial observances?

Are monastic discipline and ethical conduct receiving sufficient attention?

And perhaps most importantly, are those who passionately defend Buddhism equally committed to practising its teachings?

A thought-provoking cartoon: Protecting Buddhism or living according to Buddhism?

I recall seeing a particularly thought-provoking cartoon depicting two queues.

One was labelled “Protecting Buddhism”, while the other was labelled “Living According to the Teachings of Buddhism.” The queue for protecting Buddhism was extraordinarily long, with a large crowd eagerly waiting to demonstrate its commitment. 

In striking contrast, the queue for living according to Buddhist teachings contained only one or two people.

The cartoon was humorous, but its underlying message was profound. It highlighted an uncomfortable distinction between loudly proclaiming the need to protect a religion and quietly demonstrating its principles through one’s conduct.

Of course, a cartoon is a caricature, not a factual assessment of Buddhist society. Many Buddhists sincerely practise their religion without seeking publicity, political involvement or recognition. Nevertheless, it raises an important question: Are we sometimes more enthusiastic about defending Buddhism than about living according to the Buddha’s teachings?

Protecting Buddhism is undoubtedly important. But what precisely are we protecting if compassion, tolerance, restraint, wisdom and ethical conduct are inadequately reflected in the lives of those who profess to uphold it?

Buddhism cannot be meaningfully fostered merely through public demonstrations, political declarations, religious ceremonies or demands for constitutional protection. Its enduring strength must also come from the conduct of those who practise it.

Perhaps Sri Lanka’s greater challenge is to ensure that the queue for living according to Buddhist teachings becomes at least as long as the queue for protecting Buddhism.

This simple cartoon captures an important issue that should be central to any serious discussion about fostering the Buddha Sasana.

Ven. Kudapola Rahula Thero: A lesson from colonial history

Sri Lanka’s history provides an important example of Buddhist monks becoming involved in national affairs under circumstances profoundly different from those prevailing today.

Ven. Kudapola Rahula Thero was executed by British colonial authorities on 20 August 1848 during the suppression of the Matale Rebellion.

Thero was accused of involvement with those resisting British rule, including allegations concerning communications with rebels. He was sentenced to death by a colonial military tribunal and executed by firing squad.

The circumstances surrounding his execution and the severity of the colonial authorities’ actions subsequently attracted criticism in the British Parliament.

This episode should be understood against the broader historical background of colonial domination, resistance to foreign authority and the struggle to preserve national dignity and self-determination.

There is a fundamental distinction between confronting foreign colonial authority in circumstances involving national sovereignty and engaging in contemporary political activity primarily to preserve institutional privileges or advance partisan interests.

Today, Sri Lanka is an independent republic. Buddhism already enjoys the foremost constitutional position, and the State has an explicit responsibility to protect and foster the Buddha Sasana.

This should prompt serious reflection on the nature and purpose of contemporary religious political activism.

When Buddhist monks participate in protests and political campaigns, are they genuinely defending the Dhamma, addressing injustice and advancing the welfare of the nation?

Or are some interventions motivated principally by political allegiances, the preservation of institutional privileges or the pursuit of influence?

These questions should not be used to condemn every Buddhist monk who participates in public affairs.

Religious leaders may have legitimate reasons to speak out against injustice, corruption, violence, threats to religious freedom or actions harmful to the public welfare. Peaceful protest is a democratic right, and monks are not excluded from that right.

However, a political protest does not automatically become a defence of Buddhism simply because it is organised or led by Buddhist monks.

The interests of the nation, the interests of a political party and the interests of a religious institution are not necessarily identical.

A dispute over institutional privileges should not automatically be portrayed as an existential threat to Buddhism. Likewise, public interventions by monks should be assessed according to the principles involved, methods employed and public interest served.

The example of Ven. Kudapola Rahula Thero should encourage reflection on courage, sacrifice and national responsibility rather than serve as a blanket justification for every form of religious political activism.

The relevant question is not whether Buddhist monks should remain silent on national affairs. Rather, it is whether their interventions are guided by the Dhamma, genuine public welfare and ethical principles instead of political expediency.

Protecting the Sangha must never mean protecting misconduct

The Maha Sangha occupies a deeply respected position in Sri Lankan Buddhist society.

Throughout history, Buddhist monks have contributed enormously to preserving religious teachings, developing scholarship, advancing education and supporting communities. This contribution deserves recognition and respect.

However, respect for the Sangha should never be confused with unquestioning acceptance of the conduct of every individual monk. Instances of intimidation, incitement, violence or other unlawful behaviour must be addressed according to the law, irrespective of the religious standing of those involved.

Religious robes must never become a shield against accountability or place anyone above the law

Equally, misconduct by individual monks should not be used to discredit the wider Maha Sangha or Buddhism itself.

The distinction between the spiritual purpose of a religious institution and the behaviour of particular individuals is essential. The Buddha’s teachings emphasise compassion, wisdom, restraint, self-discipline and non-violence.

Conduct fundamentally inconsistent with these principles should not be defended merely because it is undertaken in Buddhism’s name. Indeed, public confidence in the Buddha Sasana is better strengthened through principled accountability than through unquestioning institutional protection.

Protecting Buddhism does not mean protecting wrongdoing. It means safeguarding the integrity of its teachings and the institutions entrusted with preserving them.

This is another compelling reason to examine whether the constitutional responsibility to foster the Buddha Sasana is being adequately fulfilled.

A national Buddhist Sanghayana: Turning constitutional responsibility into meaningful action

Sri Lanka could consider facilitating a national Buddhist Sanghayana, supported by the Government, as a constructive initiative towards fulfilling its constitutional duty to foster the Buddha Sasana.

Buddhist Councils, or Sangayanas, have historically played an important role in preserving, examining and reaffirming the authentic Dhamma and Vinaya.

Sri Lanka itself holds a distinguished place in the preservation of Buddhist scriptures and scholarship, including the traditional account of the Tipitaka being committed to writing at Aluvihara.

There is also an important modern precedent.

The Sixth Buddhist Council, convened in Myanmar between 1954 and 1956 with government support and participation from several Theravada Buddhist countries, including Sri Lanka, concentrated on examining, reaffirming and preserving Buddhist teachings.

Its proceedings demonstrated how government support and scholarly cooperation among Buddhist monks could contribute to preserving the Dhamma and Vinaya.

A contemporary Sri Lankan Sanghayana could bring together highly respected and learned members of the Maha Sangha representing the principal Buddhist Nikayas, supported by recognised Buddhist scholars.

Its primary religious purpose should be to reaffirm and strengthen the understanding of the Dhamma and Vinaya rather than reinterpret or compromise Buddhist teachings to accommodate temporary political or institutional interests.

However, a traditional Sanghayana could also provide the foundation for a broader, carefully structured programme aimed at strengthening the Buddha Sasana. Such a programme could address several important national priorities.

1. Strengthening monastic discipline and ethical leadership

There should be serious reflection on the observance of the Vinaya, ethical responsibilities of monastic life and the importance of maintaining public confidence in the Sangha.

Issues of monastic discipline should be addressed through credible arrangements within the relevant Buddhist traditions, while alleged criminal misconduct must remain subject to ordinary law.

2. Improving Buddhist education

The quality and effectiveness of Buddhist education should be examined, including the training of monks, development of educational resources and teaching of Buddhism to schoolchildren and lay communities.

Greater attention could be directed towards understanding the meaning and practical application of the Dhamma rather than concentrating excessively on ceremonial observance or memorisation without comprehension.

3. Engaging younger generations

Young people are growing up in a rapidly changing world influenced by technology, globalisation and changing social values.

The challenge is to communicate Buddhist teachings in ways that are understandable, intellectually meaningful and relevant to contemporary life without compromising their essential principles.

4. Encouraging the practical application of Buddhist teachings

Buddhism’s contribution to society should be reflected in compassion, non-violence, ethical decision-making, peaceful coexistence, personal responsibility and respect for others. Greater emphasis on these principles could help bridge the gap illustrated by the cartoon’s two queues.

5. Strengthening the credibility of Buddhist institutions

Responsible administration, transparent management, ethical leadership and credible processes for addressing misconduct would help strengthen confidence in Buddhist institutions. Institutional integrity is not a threat to religion. It is an important foundation for its long-term wellbeing.

6. Reflecting on the relationship between the Sangha and politics

Religious leaders should retain their freedom to express views on matters of genuine public importance.

Nevertheless, a constructive national discussion could consider how the Sangha might preserve its spiritual independence and avoid becoming closely identified with particular political parties or factional interests. This would strengthen the ability of religious leaders to speak with moral authority on issues affecting society as a whole.

7. Preserving Buddhist scholarship and cultural heritage

The preservation of manuscripts, scriptures, historical documents, ancient monasteries, archaeological sites and Buddhist scholarship should remain an important national responsibility. Digital preservation, translation, scholarly research and improved public access to authentic Buddhist teachings could form part of a long-term programme.

A Sanghayana must remain independent of political influence

An undertaking of this nature would require careful planning, respected religious leadership and scholarly credibility. The Government could provide the necessary logistical, administrative and financial assistance.

However, doctrinal deliberations should remain under the independent authority of appropriately qualified members of the Maha Sangha.

It would be counterproductive for a national Sanghayana to become another politically sponsored ceremonial event generating publicity and declarations but producing little lasting benefit. Nor should a government attempt to dictate religious doctrine or use the council to consolidate political influence over Buddhist institutions.

A sensible arrangement would distinguish the religious work of a Sanghayana from a broader programme of educational and institutional improvement.

The Sanghayana would concentrate on preserving and reaffirming the Dhamma and Vinaya, while an associated programme, developed through consultation with the Sangha and Buddhist scholars, could address contemporary educational, administrative and ethical challenges.

Its success should be judged by tangible and sustainable improvements rather than by the number of ceremonies conducted, speeches delivered or resolutions adopted.

Protecting Buddhism and respecting other religions are compatible responsibilities

Sri Lanka’s Buddhist civilisational heritage is historically significant, but recognising it should not diminish the contributions of other religious communities to the country’s national life.

Hindu, Muslim, Christian and other communities have enriched Sri Lanka through education, commerce, culture, scholarship, professional service and numerous other activities.The constitutional recognition of Buddhism’s foremost place should coexist with freedom of conscience, religious practice and equality before the law.

The European constitutional examples illustrate that special recognition of a historically established religion can exist alongside religious liberty, although the practical scope of religious equality and State neutrality varies between countries.

Sri Lanka should therefore be attentive not only to constitutional wording but also to how constitutional guarantees operate in everyday life. A country can acknowledge its Buddhist inheritance while ensuring that no citizen is treated as less deserving of dignity or legal protection because of religious belief.

The values of compassion, tolerance and respect associated with Buddhism provide a strong ethical foundation for such coexistence.

We must do more than defend Buddhism

Sri Lanka’s Buddhist heritage is too valuable to be reduced to political slogans, ceremonial declarations or disputes over constitutional status. Article 9 already gives Buddhism the foremost place and places a duty upon the State to protect and foster the Buddha Sasana. The challenge is to give meaningful effect to both parts of that responsibility.

Protecting Buddhism requires preserving its religious institutions, sacred heritage, historical traditions and freedom of practice. Fostering Buddhism requires something more demanding: strengthening understanding of the Dhamma, promoting observance of the Vinaya, improving education, encouraging ethical conduct and ensuring that Buddhist principles continue to benefit society.

The historical example of Ven. Kudapola Rahula Thero invites reflection on the difference between principled resistance to colonial authority and contemporary political interventions motivated by narrower interests.

The proposal for a national Buddhist Sanghayana offers one possible avenue for strengthening Buddhist scholarship, monastic discipline, education and institutional credibility. And the simple cartoon depicting two queues reminds us of perhaps the most important question of all.

Are we more committed to protecting Buddhism than to living according to its teachings? The future strength of Buddhism in Sri Lanka should not be measured solely by the prominence afforded to it in the Constitution, the number of temples constructed or the political influence exercised by religious institutions.

It should also be measured by how faithfully the Dhamma is understood, how consistently the Vinaya is observed and how meaningfully Buddhist values are reflected in everyday conduct.

Protecting Buddhism safeguards our inheritance. Fostering Buddhism ensures that this inheritance remains meaningful for future generations. Ultimately, the most effective protection of Buddhism will come not merely from those who defend it most loudly, but from those who demonstrate its teachings most faithfully.

Sri Lanka must certainly protect its Buddhist heritage. But our greater challenge is to ensure that the queue for living according to the Buddha’s teachings becomes at least as long as the queue for protecting Buddhism.

title: Dileepa doctrine, Buddhist revivalism, Opposition predicaments, left prospects | Daily FT
