ASG Dileepa Peiris, PC

Why does the AKD administration want peacetime ‘anti-terrorism’ legislation (PSTA) far wider in scope than JR Jayewardene’s wartime PTA? 

Because in a pre-emptive strike, it is constructing a matrix of new repressive legislation to shut the system, constricting democratic space and suffocating critical social expression, while:

The evening of the confrontation outside the Secretariat between Buddhist monks and presidential staff plus Police, TV news showed senior JVP personality, Minister K.D. Lal Kantha addressing a public meeting, declaring: 

“…they think that we are going to leave after the next three years. I can tell you we are not going to leave after the next three years!” 

The PSTA segues into the ‘Organised Crime’ Bill (POCA) which is an organised crime itself. If the terrible triptych of PSTA-POCA-NGO legislation is erected, Sri Lanka will no longer be a functioning democracy. 

But, as Nietzsche said about God, if democracy is dead, the Government having killed it, “then everything is permitted”. From Locke to Lenin, that means ‘all forms of struggle’ become legitimate.

Dileepa dictum

The Colombo Chief Magistrate Asanga S. Bodaragama did the cause of justice and social peace a service when he ruled that former First Lady Shiranthi Rajapaksa be granted bail on the basis of the special circumstances that had been drawn to his notice—the report of medical doctors of the Colombo National Hospital, signed by the hospital’s Director that Madam Rajapaksa required a coronary bypass surgery soon. 

In contradistinction, as the TV news showed that evening, ASG Dileepa Peiris, PC, representing the State, contended that despite the medical report which recommended a bypass operation, Shiranthi Rajapaksa should not be released on bail because the need did not arise as she was already warded at the National Hospital.   

This illustrates the thinking of State apparatchiks in the time of AKD Chinthanaya. Though there was an exit ramp offered in a fraught situation by the possibility of bail, ASG Peiris thought it should not be taken because it need not be. He didn’t regard the medically confirmed need for cardiac surgery to constitute a sufficiently special circumstance for the 73-year-old former First Lady—hardly accused of murder—to be released from custody on bail. He didn’t have the heart to agree that a heart bypass should warrant being able to go home to her husband and family before the invasive surgery.

Dileepa Peiris also seemed to assume that the former First Lady would automatically opt to undergo surgery at the National Hospital or should not have the right to opt for a private hospital and surgeon of her choice. 

The high-profile, hard-charging representative of the AG’s Department obviously wasn’t anxious to park this hot potato of an issue somewhere safe, and buy time. Had the AG’s Department stand carried the day, the 73-year-old former First Lady would have incurred all the risks of heart surgery while remaining a prisoner in the custody of the State. If something untoward happened, it would have been on the State’s watch. Dileepa Peiris’ recommendation was hardly an exemplary calculus of the risk to the larger interests of the State which he serves. 


Luckily for all concerned, Colombo Chief Magistrate Bodaragama held the balance and ruled wisely, deftly steering clear of a possible human tragedy with wide-ranging moral, ethical, social and political ramifications for legitimacy and stability. But not before we had televised confirmation of the unreasonable, reckless argumentation of ASG Dileepa Peiris, which exemplified the polarising, de-stabilising brutalisation of thought and discourse within the institutions of the State during the Dissanayake Presidency and JVP-NPP rule.

Sinhala-Buddhist network

The fairly sizeable knot of Bhikkhus and lay persons gathered outside the Presidential Secretariat could not be compared to the crowds that swarmed the Galle Face Green ‘Gota Go Gama’ sit-down, let alone the double-tap ‘tsunami’ waves of the Aragalaya. 

Cost-of-living pressures, student/education grievances and democracy/governance issues generate far vaster multitudes than religio-cultural issues—the evidence is clear from Paris, Marseilles, Lyon, Madrid, Milan, Turin, Tunis and Tirana. Half-a-million demonstrated in France. 

That said, the Bhikkhu-led mobilisation and the Government’s zero-tolerance eviction showed that the administration now faces a new front of discontent, which can grow. 

The Bhikkhu demonstration was far more impressive upstream, coming into Colombo from Kandy through the towns and suburbs, than it was at nightfall at Galle Face or later at Vihara Maha Devi Park. The response of the nodal Buddhist temples along the way and the supportive laity showed a strong vein of religio-cultural and perhaps ultranationalist discontent at the President and Government, outside Colombo city. The march and the reception at the temples showed an actual or potential social network of religio-cultural dissent and mobilisation. 

The Government has lost the Sinhala-Buddhist middle classes, largely suburban, preponderating in what Prof. Kumar David dubbed ‘the Dharmapala Belt’. It is the stratum that broke from Ranil’s UNP and voted for the Hela Urumaya variants led by S.L. Gunasekara and Champika Ranawake. Together with the MEP constituency of Dinesh Gunawardena, they constitute the Sinhala-Buddhist intermediate strata which may split unevenly between Namal’s SLPP (probably backed by Weerawansa-Gammanpila), Dilith Jayaweera’s Sarvajana, and Champika Ranawake, but are decidedly alienated from AKD-JVP-NPP.

SLPP dilemmas

The SLPP is in better shape—more spirited, efficient, determined—than anyone would think, given that its young leader is in jail and several other personalities are being hauled up before the courts. It has not been reduced to a residue of hardcore voters, and is capable of attracting new young professional talent including in the Colombo District. It is more flexible and open than the larger SJB.    

What the SLPP really has going for it—unlike the SJB—is a narrative, a coherent ‘story’ which is at the core of soft power, and which it holds the franchise for: the heroic narrative of Mahinda Rajapaksa, the war and post-war development; the pathos of the persecution of Mahinda, his family and the war-winning military brass by an unpatriotic, incompetent ruler and administration; the hope centred on the cool courage of the imprisoned affable young Namal Rajapaksa.  

That said, the SLPP has a political dilemma to resolve, namely how to retrieve its progressive centre-left character, return to the Rajapaksa middle path legacy, and focus on winning back the rural peasant base lost by the fertilizer fiasco, while retaining the Sinhala-Buddhist nationalist constituency. 

When Sirimavo Bandaranaike and her coalition swept to a landslide victory in 1970, she won the Catholic belt which she had lost in the early 1960s. She always had a sizeable Muslim vote (through personalities like Badiuddin Muhamed, Halim Ishak, Alavi Moulana). Chandrika won the minority vote in 1994 and 1999. Mahinda won in 2005 and 2010 with the Catholic and Muslim vote. However, MR lost in 2015 because he lost both minorities, Muslim and Christian—not due to him, but to an ultranationalist deviation in the State, Government and party. 


If the SLPP runs on its 2019 agenda and discourse, fails to rebalance and retrieve MR’s minority vote of 2005 and 2010, it runs a huge risk in a three-way split in the majority vote, making the minority vote a decisive variable. 

Before his incarceration, Namal Rajapaksa was successfully rebuilding the party’s rural peasant base—which may explain the timing of his arrest. The SLPP must wisely navigate the Ven. Gnanasara issue and the agitation around it, while never forgetting the top priority of winning back:

The real dilemma for the SLPP will be the 13th Amendment and Provincial Councils. 

MR was always for PCs and held elections even under conditions unfavourable to him in and out of wartime. Unlike MR’s SLFP, the SLPP has hawks around and within it who are anti-13A/PCs. 

What if the AKD administration plays the card of a new Constitution or legislation which entrenches itself in power by extending its term of office, while dropping the 13th Amendment and PCs? What if it comes to a referendum? Would the SLPP campaign for a ‘NO’ vote as it should—or will it, its allies and voters be confused by 13A abolition, and thereby unwittingly help the Government win?

SJB’s ‘thin’ narrative

The SJB has declared that it is for the full implementation of the 13th Amendment including powers over land and the Police. It hasn’t drawn the distinction between full implementation and immediate implementation. This problematic, contentious pair of powers should be devolved incrementally and conditionally. 

Sajith and the SJB could lose the election only on this issue alone— the unconditional pledge of land and Police powers—just as Sir John Kotelawela lost on the language issue, and Dudley Senanayake was besieged, his 7-party coalition Government split and utterly defeated in 1970 also because of the opaque Dudley-Chelvanayakam ‘District Councils’ agreement.  

The SJB has also been for the abolition of the executive Presidency. How is that compatible with its recent commemoration of JR Jayewardene? JR’s Open Economy cannot be commended while simultaneously opposing the Executive Presidency because JR himself made explicit that the Presidency was a political prerequisite for the Open Economy; they were two sides of one paradigm.   

More perplexing is how the SJB intends to support and implement 13A in full, without the executive Presidency which acts as both over-watch and guardrail, and in the absence of which 13A flips the character of the Constitution over into federalism.   

If AKD produces a draft Constitution which removes 13A, dilutes the system of proportional representation to a mixed system, substitutes an executive Prime Ministership (as in Israel or Germany’s Chancellorship) for the current Presidency, insists that the Government’s term of office commences with the promulgation of the new Constitution (as Madam Bandaranaike’s Government did, stretching two years beyond its mandate), how would the SJB campaign at the referendum? For an unambiguous NO vote as it should, or will its confusion send mixed signals which enable the Government to win the referendum and remain beyond 2029?   

Having inexplicably failed to commemorate President Premadasa’s birth centenary—with its utterly compelling narrative potential—in the crucial election year 2024, the SJB has no unique ‘origin story’ or identity. Its narrative reckons its parentage/ lineage from Ranil’s UNP, not Premadasa’s. It is ambivalent and ambiguous as to what, why, and how far it opposes AKD’s economic model which is an extreme extension of Ranil’s. However, if the SJB followed President Premadasa’s economic paradigm, it would be frontally opposing AKD’s.

It is silent on the crudity and coarseness of the treatment of the Rajapaksas, exultantly exclaiming ‘these are cases initiated against crooks by our Government’. That insensitivity will ensure the SJB doesn’t secure a fraction of the Rajapaksa ‘patriotic-populist’ vote which went JVP-NPP in 2024. 

The SJB lacks the realism to discern that the vote—mainly centre-left nationalist Rajapaksa/SLPP—which swung to AKD-JVP-NPP in 2024, cannot be won over by the SJB or SJB-UNP as they stand, but needs a radical pivot to (Ranasinghe) Premadasa’s progressive-populism by which he beat Mrs. Bandaranaike in 1988 by attracting the poorer voters from the SLFP and JVP constituencies.     

The SJB is trapped between:

So far the SJB hasn’t done or said anything about the incoming draconian legislation, the PSTA, POCA etc. Currently, the main Opposition party is irresponsibly inactive, exhibiting inertia. It makes marginal intervention in the national crisis and exercises little attraction on the public imagination.   

The SJB should stop behaving as if the rival Rajapaksa-led SLPP rather than the ruling JVP-NPP is its main adversary. 

While the rest of the Opposition must recognise that the SJB is the largest Opposition shareholder and is indispensable, the SJB must realise that while it is the largest single Opposition shareholder and as such is indispensable, it is also utterly inadequate in and of itself.

Vasu’s whitewash

Emeritus leftist Vasudeva Nanayakkara launched a memoir recently, and has repeatedly extended his support to the present Government, urging others to follow suit. This is ironic because Vasudeva was best known and respected as a leftist dissident within the United Front Government of 1970-1977, rather than as a conformist supporter of it. 

Vasu has suppressed the lesson of his own experience. He was swept away together with the entire left leadership in 1977 because he supported and stayed with the Government while dissenting. But he was re-elected to parliament relatively soon, as was Sarath Muttetuwegama, and unlike the LSSP-CPSL leaders who died exiled from Parliament, because he, like Sarath, had conspicuously dissented. 

The lesson is: with mounting mass economic hardship, quit the Government and form/join a left alternative such as the CPI-M constituted in India, or if you stay, rebel, otherwise you’ll sink like the LSSP-CPSL in 1977.

FSP-PSA filling the vacuum

While the Bhikkhu mobilisation was attracting attention, there was an entirely different type of protest on the streets that week. Most significant was a demonstration on a rainy night by a large number of spirited medical students who came up against a police presence.

The Inter-University Students Federation (IUSF), historically a JVP stronghold, had been supportive of the Frontline Socialist Party (FSP) for many years. The IUSF’s zenith was under the leadership of Wasantha Mudalige, when it was the decisive driving force of the Aragalaya which overthrew Gotabaya Rajapaksa.  

After the 2024 victory the JVP dented the IUSF by co-opting the Peradeniya University medical students. Now, the medical students (or a majority) have returned to the revitalised FSP’s sphere of ideological influence. Days before the medical students the IUSF too was back on the streets. 

With the SJB’s inactivity outside Parliament, the only forces on the streets are the religio-cultural nationalists and the FSP and its partner, the People’s Struggle Alliance (Jana Aragala Vyaparaya). If not for the FSP-PSA, it would only be the religio-cultural resistance of a ‘retro’ character, which would be unhealthy. 

When the JVP-NPP Governmentt inevitably suffers its own ‘1977’ defeat, sincere supporters can evacuate to the FSP, undergo ideological rectification, consolidating a Left Opposition whichever mainstream party forms the Government.   

With the SJB and the SLPP hamstrung by their intersection with this or that subset of AKD-JVP-NPP policy (economic ‘reform’, 13A abolition respectively), we are nearing the type of exceptional ‘portal’ through which a left alternative can grow exponentially, if it incorporates and fulfils the oppositional roles and tasks that the mainstream ‘bourgeois’ parties have historically undertaken but have now abandoned. 

This ‘leap’ requires a ‘national-popular’ (Gramsci) bloc and strategy drawn from the left realism of the communist tradition’s ‘central current’: Lenin, Gramsci, Dimitrov, Togliatti, Mao and Ho Chi Minh.

title: Another IMF program in 2028? | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 22 October 2026 00:22

Sri Lanka faces a defining economic choice. As its current four-year IMF program approaches its scheduled conclusion in March 2027, debate is growing over whether the country should seek another program in 2028 or attempt to sustain its recovery without one.

The question is not simply whether Sri Lanka needs the IMF. It is whether the country can convert economic stabilisation into lasting prosperity, reduce poverty and create opportunities for its people. The IMF program has helped restore stability, credibility, strengthen reserves and advance debt restructuring. Yet significant debt vulnerabilities remain, and sustainable growth requires reforms that go beyond fiscal targets .Sri Lanka must move beyond managing its crisis to building an economy that can prevent the next one.

Debt discipline

Fiscal discipline cannot be abandoned. Sri Lanka must maintain credible public finances, manage debt-service obligations and rebuild buffers against external shocks. Walking away from the IMF without a credible alternative financing strategy could weaken investor confidence and expose the economy to renewed pressure.

However, fiscal consolidation cannot become an end in itself. A government can improve its accounts while households struggle, businesses postpone investment and skilled young people leave. If economic recovery does not translate into better living standards and reduced poverty, its sustainability will remain in question.

The World Bank’s October 2026 Sri Lanka Development Update estimated that 16.9% of the population lived below its $ 4.20-a-day poverty threshold in 2025, compared with 11.5% in 2019. It projects poverty to decline gradually, but remain above pre-crisis levels through 2028. These estimates underline a fundamental weakness in measuring success through macroeconomic indicators alone: the economy can recover before household welfare does. The tax burden deserves particular attention. Individuals pay income tax on earnings and then face consumption taxes when spending their after-tax income. Consumption taxes can disproportionately affect lower-income households, which spend a greater share of their earnings on essentials. Businesses also face multiple taxes and levies, although corporate income tax is generally applied to taxable profits.

The objective should be a broader, fairer and more efficient tax base, not simply higher collections. Public expenditure must deliver better services, waste and inefficient spending must be addressed, and social protection must reach vulnerable households. Citizens are more likely to support fiscal discipline when they can see tangible results.

FDI opportunity

Sri Lanka cannot achieve sustainable debt reduction through taxation and expenditure cuts alone. It needs faster economic growth, stronger exports and substantial investment in productive capacity.

Foreign direct investment (FDI) can bring capital, technology, management expertise, access to international markets and higher-value employment. Yet investors need predictable policies, efficient approvals, competitive energy costs, reliable infrastructure and confidence that rules will not change arbitrarily.

Sri Lanka should target investment in export manufacturing, IT and business services, logistics, tourism, renewable energy and agribusiness. Investment promotion must translate into implementation: fewer bureaucratic delays, transparent incentives and accountability for delivering projects.

Crucially, FDI should generate productive jobs, raise incomes and expand opportunities beyond a narrow segment of society. Growth matters, but who benefits from that growth matters equally.

The battle to retain talent

Perhaps Sri Lanka’s greatest economic risk is losing the people needed to drive its recovery. When skilled professionals, entrepreneurs and ambitious young people leave, the country loses productive capacity, innovation and part of its future tax base. Remittances support foreign-exchange earnings, but cannot fully replace the economic value of a skilled workforce building businesses at home.

Retaining talent requires more than appeals to patriotism. Young people need competitive salaries, merit-based career progression, opportunities to innovate and confidence that enterprise will be rewarded. They must be able to see a future in Sri Lanka.

This is where FDI, education, labour reform, employment and poverty reduction intersect. Investors need skilled workers; skilled workers need productive employers; and growing businesses create jobs that can lift families into more secure livelihoods. Better technical education, vocational training and stronger links between education and industry are essential.

The ultimate test of recovery is not merely how much the economy grows, but how many people escape poverty, find productive employment and gain a genuine stake in the country’s future.

2028 and beyond

Sri Lanka should neither rule out another IMF program nor assume one is inevitable. The decision must depend on financing needs, debt-service capacity, reserve adequacy, market access and the credibility of the domestic policy framework.

Before the current program ends, the Government should establish measurable targets for investment, exports, productivity, quality employment, poverty reduction and tax fairness alongside fiscal and debt objectives. Progress should be publicly monitored.

The real measure of success is not whether Sri Lanka signs another IMF agreement in 2028. It is whether the country has built an economy in which investors want to invest, businesses can grow, poverty declines and young people choose to stay. The IMF can provide a framework for stability, but it cannot substitute for strong institutions, creativity, innovation, sound economic management and private-sector dynamism. Sri Lanka’s ultimate objective must be to make external assistance a choice rather than a recurring necessity, ensuring that economic recovery delivers dignity, opportunity and shared prosperity for all. With its human talent, entrepreneurial spirit and strategic advantages, Sri Lanka has every potential to achieve this—and to do so with confidence and dignity.

For a long time, I believed social media had democratised truth. Everyone could speak and report. Information was instant, free, and everywhere.

Today, I believe it has democratised something else: misinformation, which is, in most cases, fantasy-driven. Therefore, I have made a conscious decision: I am going back to traditional media.

I am returning to the daily newspaper, its morning editorial, and the thrill of turning pages. To reports filed by reliable sources, by journalists who put their names, their reputations, and their organisations behind what they write. To dabble in my daily appetite for the Crossword puzzle. What changed?

A realisation. On social media, falsehoods spread faster than the truth. A fake video can travel across the world before the correction has had time to put its shoes on. AI-generated images, out-of-context content and clips, and anonymous accounts claiming to be "insiders" — the ecosystem now rewards outrage, not accuracy.

We are no longer debating opinions. We are debating facts. And that is dangerous. I have seen CEOs lose their reputations, markets crash on rumours, and entire communities polarise over an unverified post, often half-baked. And what about the glorified 'citizen journalist'?

A decade ago, we celebrated the idea that everyone with a phone is a journalist. It sounded democratic. Today, that title has lost its standing. Without training, accountability, or an editor to ask "is this true?", the citizen journalist often becomes simply a citizen amplifier — amplifying outrage, rumour, and half-truths for likes. 

 Journalism is not just posting what you saw; it is verifying it. We've lost that discipline, so I am going back to professionals who still practise it. Social media has given us speed, but it has taken away verification.

Why traditional media still matters. I don't agree with every editorial. No newspaper is perfect. But traditional media has something social media has lost: accountability. There is an editor. There is a publisher. There is a correction policy. Process: A story is checked, sourced, and legally reviewed before it is printed. Patience: It values being right over being first.

When I read a credible daily, I may not get the news first, but I trust I am getting it right. So, my personal rule from now on: If it's important — a business decision, a geopolitical event, or a health issue — I will not rely on a viral post. I will wait for a reliable source to confirm it.

Speed is cheap. Truth is expensive. I choose truth. The future belongs to AI, but truth will still belong to those who do the hard work of journalism. I invite you to do the same: Read less from the feed. Read more from
the paper.

title: Sri Lanka’s new compliance era: Why MSMEs should consider incorporation | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 22 October 2026 00:20
-     - 44

A changing business environment

Sri Lanka’s economic reform program, 

 supported by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), is bringing significant changes to the country’s tax policy, revenue administration, statutory compliance and digital infrastructure. While these reforms aim to strengthen public revenue, improve transparency and support economic stability, they also require businesses to reconsider how they organise, manage and protect their operations.

Changes in direct taxation and indirect taxation, amendments to tax laws, the expansion of digital tax administration, the introduction of prescribed TIN Certificate procedures for specified transactions and the move towards paperless Customs declarations are transforming the compliance environment in which businesses operate.

For Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), these developments raise a fundamental question: Is continuing to operate as a sole proprietorship or traditional partnership still the most appropriate business structure, or should more entrepreneurs consider conducting their operations through a private limited liability company?

As a Chartered Accountant and Tax and Management Consultant, I believe this question deserves serious consideration. For many growth-oriented MSMEs, incorporation should no longer be viewed merely as a formality required when a business becomes large. It should be considered an important measure of risk management, governance and long-term sustainability.

The traditional MSME business model and its risks

A significant number of Sri Lankan entrepreneurs establish their businesses as sole proprietorships or partnerships. These structures are familiar, relatively straightforward to establish and may involve fewer administrative formalities at the outset.

For a very small enterprise with limited transactions and low commercial risk, such an arrangement may initially be practical. However, the position can change significantly as turnover increases, employees are recruited, credit facilities are obtained, imports and exports expand, and contractual relationships become more complex.

A critical distinction concerns the legal separation between the business and its owner.

In a sole proprietorship, the owner and the business are not separate legal persons. Business debts and other liabilities can therefore expose the proprietor’s personal assets, subject to the applicable law and circumstances.

In a traditional partnership, partners may also face personal exposure for partnership obligations. A disagreement between partners, an unauthorised transaction, a contractual default or a financial liability arising from business operations can consequently affect the personal financial position of the individuals concerned.

This risk becomes particularly important when a business experiences a cash-flow crisis, accumulates tax arrears, defaults on a bank facility or faces legal action from suppliers, customers or other creditors.

The proprietor may believe that the business is a small family operation, but the law does not necessarily separate personal wealth from business liabilities simply because the enterprise operates on a small scale.

The central issue is not merely how much profit a business earns. It is also the extent of personal financial exposure its owners are prepared to accept.

Compliance is entering a more demanding phase

Sri Lanka’s evolving tax and regulatory environment makes this question even more relevant.

The Inland Revenue (Amendment) Act, No. 11 of 2026, introduces a new prosecution mechanism under section 185A for specified failures to comply with statutory tax obligations, including failures to file prescribed statements or returns, register with the Commissioner-General where required, or appear before the Commissioner-General in compliance with a notice issued under section 123. The Commissioner-General must first issue written notice allowing 30 days for compliance. Failure to comply with the notice without reasonable cause can result in prosecution. Upon conviction, the penalty may be a fine of up to Rs. 400,000, imprisonment for up to six months, or both.

These provisions should not be interpreted as meaning that every tax error automatically results in criminal proceedings. Nevertheless, they demonstrate why businesses must treat statutory filing, registration and related compliance obligations seriously.

The same Act also requires every company incorporated or registered in Sri Lanka to register with the Commissioner-General of Inland Revenue within 30 days of incorporation or registration. This obligation is distinct from the TIN Certificate submission procedure applying to specified individual transactions.

Furthermore, the IRD’s Circular No. SEC/2026/E/07, dated 22 September 2026, prescribes procedures for TIN Certificate verification in specified transactions from 1 November 2026, subject to the stated exemptions.

In parallel, Sri Lanka Customs made the paperless Customs Declaration process at the Declaration Directorate (Long Room) mandatory from 1 October 2026. Importers and declarants are required to submit Customs Declarations and supporting documents using valid digital signatures. Manual processing and submission are no longer accepted under this procedure.

These developments form part of a broader shift towards electronic records, digital verification, more structured reporting and stronger compliance controls.

For MSMEs, the practical consequence is clear: maintaining reliable accounting records, reconciling transactions, meeting filing deadlines and preserving documentary evidence are becoming increasingly important.

A business that relies entirely on informal bookkeeping, personal bank accounts, incomplete invoices and undocumented arrangements between family members may find it increasingly difficult to demonstrate compliance when required.

Why a private limited company deserves serious consideration

Under the Companies Act, No. 7 of 2007, a company incorporated under the Act becomes a body corporate in its registered name. Section 87 also establishes that a shareholder is not liable for an act, default or obligation of the company merely because that person is a shareholder.

This legal separation is a major advantage of incorporation.

A private limited company can enter into contracts, own assets, maintain bank accounts, employ staff and conduct business in its own name. Its financial records and obligations can be distinguished from those of its shareholders.

Subject to the applicable law and circumstances, this separation can provide shareholders with an important layer of protection against ordinary business liabilities incurred by the company.

Consider an MSME engaged in wholesale trading. The business may maintain substantial inventory, purchase goods on credit, employ workers, lease premises and borrow funds from a bank. If the business experiences serious financial difficulties, the distinction between company liabilities and the personal affairs of its shareholders may become extremely important.

Operating through a properly managed private limited company can help establish that distinction, provided the business is genuinely conducted through the company and its legal and financial affairs are maintained separately.

For entrepreneurs who have accumulated personal assets over many years, protecting those assets from ordinary commercial risks is a legitimate part of responsible business planning.

Limited liability is protection, not immunity

It is essential, however, to understand that incorporation does not eliminate every form of personal liability.

A private limited company is not a mechanism for avoiding tax obligations, concealing assets or disregarding statutory requirements. Its principal advantage is that it establishes a separate legal entity and generally separates shareholder liability from the company’s obligations.

That protection does not necessarily extend to a director or shareholder who gives a personal guarantee for a bank loan, commits fraud, acts unlawfully, breaches an independent legal duty or becomes personally liable under another applicable legal provision.

The Companies Act itself imposes duties on directors. Sections 187, 188 and 189 address acting in good faith in the company’s interests, compliance with the Act and the company’s articles, and the required standard of care.

Directors must therefore take their responsibilities seriously. They cannot assume that the company structure provides immunity from the consequences of their own conduct.

Similarly, a company’s incorporation does not automatically absolve an individual from personal responsibilities arising under tax, employment, environmental, regulatory or other applicable laws.

The correct professional message is therefore not that incorporation removes all personal risk. It is that a properly structured and properly managed company can provide a more effective legal separation between business risk and personal wealth than an unincorporated business generally provides.

Incorporation can also improve business governance

The benefits extend beyond liability protection.

First, incorporation encourages a clearer separation between business finances and personal expenditure. Maintaining separate bank accounts, recording amounts introduced by shareholders, documenting withdrawals and reconciling transactions can improve financial discipline.

Second, a company structure supports more formal documentation of ownership, management responsibilities, contracts and business decisions. This can be particularly useful in family businesses where informal arrangements may otherwise create misunderstandings. Third, incorporation can improve the business’s readiness to approach banks, investors, suppliers and larger customers. A properly maintained company profile, financial statements and accounting records can support due diligence and make the business easier to assess.

Fourth, a company may provide a more practical framework for succession planning, changes in ownership and continuity when a founder retires or a family member takes over management.

Finally, incorporation encourages owners to distinguish between their roles as shareholders, directors and employees. This can improve accountability and help professionalise a business that has outgrown an owner-managed informal structure.

These advantages do not arise automatically upon registration. They depend on proper implementation, consistent record-keeping and responsible management.

Does incorporation automatically reduce tax?

One misconception must be addressed directly: a private limited company is not automatically more tax-efficient than a sole proprietorship or partnership.

The appropriate tax outcome depends on the nature of the business, taxable profits, remuneration paid to owners, dividends, financing arrangements, applicable tax rates and other relevant provisions.

A company may face additional accounting, secretarial, filing and administrative expenses. It must maintain its statutory records and comply with the obligations applicable to its legal form. Financial statement and audit requirements must also be considered according to the relevant law and any applicable exemptions.

Consequently, the decision to incorporate should not be based solely on a perceived tax advantage.

A proper assessment should compare the existing business structure with the proposed company structure, taking into account tax consequences, compliance costs, expected growth, personal liability exposure, financing needs and long-term objectives.

The objective should be to select the structure that best supports the enterprise’s commercial requirements while maintaining statutory compliance.

A practical strategy for MSMEs

I recommend that MSME owners undertake a structured review of their business position before deciding whether to incorporate.

The review should consider the scale and nature of operations, annual turnover, borrowings, contractual commitments, inventory and other assets, number of employees, tax exposure, regulatory obligations and the potential consequences of business failure.

Businesses involved in wholesale and retail trading, manufacturing, construction, importing and exporting, security services, professional services and other activities involving substantial contractual or financial commitments should give particular attention to the risks inherent in their current structure. Where incorporation is appropriate, the transition should be properly planned. Business assets, contracts, stock, licences, employees, bank facilities and tax registrations should be reviewed to determine how they should be dealt with under the new company.

Owners should also establish appropriate accounting systems, separate banking arrangements, internal controls, tax-compliance calendars and clear responsibilities for directors and management.

Professional advice from a Chartered Accountant, tax adviser, company secretary and legal adviser, where appropriate, can help ensure that the transition is carried out correctly.

A balanced recommendation, not a one-size-fits-all rule

It would be inappropriate to suggest that every small business must immediately become a private limited company. A low-risk enterprise operating on a very small scale may reasonably continue as a sole proprietorship if the owner understands the risks and the arrangement remains commercially suitable.

However, when a business begins to employ people, borrow substantially, accumulate valuable assets, enter significant contracts, engage in international trade or expand beyond the founder’s direct control, its legal structure should be reconsidered.

Incorporation is particularly worth considering when the personal assets of the proprietor or partners are increasingly exposed to risks arising from the business.

The decision must be based on the individual circumstances of the enterprise—not merely its turnover or the desire to adopt a more impressive business name.

Conclusion: formalise the business before risk dictates the decision

Sri Lanka’s evolving tax and regulatory environment is changing the way businesses must operate. Digital tax administration, stronger enforcement, more structured reporting and paperless Customs procedures are making documentation, accountability and timely compliance increasingly important.

For MSMEs, the response should go beyond employing better accounting software or engaging a tax consultant to prepare returns. It should include a fundamental assessment of the legal structure through which the business operates.

My professional recommendation is that growth-oriented Sri Lankan MSMEs should seriously consider conducting their operations through a properly managed private limited company, where the benefits of legal separation, governance, continuity and risk management justify the additional costs and obligations.

The objective is not to avoid statutory responsibilities. It is to establish a structure in which those responsibilities are clearly recognised, properly managed and supported by reliable records.

A sustainable business needs more than profitability. It needs sound governance, a disciplined compliance culture and an appropriate legal structure to protect the enterprise’s future—and, within the limits of the law, the personal wealth of the people who built it.

title: Feminist Collective for Economic Justice condemns NPP’s oppressive laws amidst regressive economic policies | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 22 October 2026 00:00
-     - 10

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake

The Feminist Collective for Economic Justice (FCEJ) in a statement has condemned the oppressive laws, particularly the most recent Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill (PSTA) and the Organised Crime Bill, proposed by the Government in October 2026. 

Following is the full statement of FCEJ, a collective of feminist economists, scholars, feminist activists, university students and lawyers that came together in April 2022 to understand, analyse and give voice to policy recommendations based on lived realities in the current economic crisis in Sri Lanka.

While addressing crime and terrorism, is a legitimate objective of a Government, the unprecedented criminalisation of poverty, expansion of broad policing power and the usurpation of the people’s judicial power are extremely concerning. 

We believe that a closer look at the context reveals whose interests this legislative agenda serves. Authoritarianism fuelled by right wing fearmongering along the lines of terrorism, criminalising migrants, minorities and the poor, and condemning countries of the global south as corrupt and indisciplined, is a global trend that protects wealth and wealth making. Similarly, economic policies that favour the wealthy have always required the strong police powers of the state to counter the dissent, disgruntlement, desperation and violence that are products of exploitation of labour and environment on the lives of ordinary people. It is clear that economic policies are driven by corporate greed in the form of a rapidly expanding export sector, mineral mining, land intensive green transitioning, financialisation and privatisation of essential public services. 

The intensifying crisis upon the lives of the poor and working people of the country is all too visible. Economic insecurity of households prevails with continued low wages, increasing wage theft and increased cost of living. This has led to the expansion of household debt and exploitation of the working poor by predatory financial institutions. Precarious informal labour has expanded, increasing harassment and exploitation in the workplace. These stresses are compounded by the impact of climate change on access to water, agriculture and fishing livelihoods and on working conditions in plantations and factories, thus increasing economic burdens on families recovering from recurrent climate crises. There is widespread desperation to make ends meet, hold on to work, find multiple sources of income to feed one’s family, and thus the compulsion to migrate for work.

Anti-people economic policies

It is in the context of a growing frustration of ordinary people that the NPP Government commits to expediting economic policies of privatisation of essential services and continues to borrow foreign loans with conditionalities that work against its people. The NPP has continued austerity measures with removal of subsidies, low public spending and diminishing social security. It is pursuing private foreign investment without adequate protections for labour and environment as seen in the rush to implement large scale projects for mining, solar farms, wind power, palm oil plantations, and special economic zones. The corporate capture of the State is enabling bulldozing by an elite agenda that is pursuing wealth at the cost of people. It does so in the name of economic stability and fighting corruption. It is an economic trend driven by forces that are well aware of peoples’ hardship and desperation, and anticipates public protest and agitation. And so the ‘enemy’ is created and resisted by the State.  It is the citizen protestor complaining of hardships and demanding the Government steps down, the worker engaged in strike action that slows down production and the environmental activist who resists large scale projects by foreign investors, who are cast in the role of ‘enemy’. Anti people economic agendas have always been accompanied by oppressive laws.

Anti-people laws

We are witnessing a rapid increase in the number of oppressive laws presented and passed under the NPP Government In October 2026, we saw the Government present the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill (PSTA), which seeks to repeal and replace the Prevention of Terrorism Act of 1979. The Bill proposes a wider definition of ‘terrorism’ that potentially considers all forms of political opposition, rallies, protests and acts that ‘compel a Government or international organisation to do or abstain from doing any act’, as terrorism. The Bill proposes broad powers to the police, armed forces and coastguard, unprecedented power to the President in relation to proscribing organisations,  unprecedented power to the Attorney General to settlements whereby prosecutions are deferred in return for public apologies or reparations, and restricts judicial supervision over arrests and detention. The PSTA lacks meaningful safeguards and access to justice for those against whom such laws have been arbitrarily or illegally used.

The Prevention of Organised Crime Bill introduces powers similar to those in the PSTA and additionally allows for confessions before police officers to be used in court. The confession clause is reminiscent of the same in the PTA that led to torture and cruel and degrading treatment of detainees to obtain confessions which were later used as the only evidence to convict and punish persons. Similarly the Prevention of Foreign Terrorist Fighters Bill applies to citizens and non-citizens who participate in offences which are, once again, so broadly defined, encapsulating acts which may be far removed from the core offence of ‘terrorism’.  

The proposed NGO Bill demands mandatory registration of all voluntary social activities including of any groups of five or more working together, notification for any crowdfunding, imposes a duty on Non Governmental Organisations to align with Government policy, fines up to a maximum of one million rupees for administrative wrongdoings and lapses such as failing to provide information,  and overall restricts freedom of association and expression.

In 2026 alone this Government passed the Convention on the Suppression of Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Act, The Prevention of Money Laundering (Amendment) Act and Financial Transactions Reporting (Amendment) Act, creating legalised intrusion into privacy and State surveillance. The Microfinance and Credit Regulatory Authority Act of 2026 also dismantles community savings and fails to institute meaningful safeguards against exploitation of indebtedness, which in itself has significant socio-economic consequences. These laws are new legislative layers over an existing oppressive legislative landscape such as the Online Safety Act, the ICCPR Act, the Prevention of Terrorism Act and the Public Security Ordinance, and the plethora of colonial penal legislation that has been consistently deployed against a democratically and peacefully protesting public. The scheme and tone of all these laws is one of consolidating power, controlling people and expanding the power of officials to penalise citizen activity.

Listen to people and change course

In the two years the National People’s Power (NPP) has been in Government after being elected with an overwhelming mandate for system change, we have witnessed the continuation of the oppressive laws and burdensome economic policies of Wickremesinghe’s two year stint. The NPP has opted for macroeconomic stability at the expense of increased precarity for the common people, especially working women who are shouldering the burden. 

The pile up of all these oppressive laws accompanying economic policies that have and will continue to fail people is not a coincidence. It is chilling to watch the changing legislative landscape, without adequate explanation or justification and without any real consideration of public opinion or feedback. 

We recall that it was in the late 1970s under the leadership of J R Jayawardene and the aggressive drive to liberalise the economy that development and deployment of a scheme of oppressive laws (Public Security Ordinance, Essential Services Act, Prevention of Terrorism Act) with similar intensity was last deployed.

We call out the anti-people project of the NPP Government. You were voted in on a mandate to specifically reverse exploitation and oppression. You are failing to hear the ordinary people of Sri Lanka, you are failing to see the irreversible impact of the economic policies and police powers on the most vulnerable, you are promising those who support you a better life while building institutions of oppression that will work against their welfare, and your actions serve elite interests in the name of macro-economic stability and growth. Change course, it’s already too late.

The award also recognises a broader approach to hospitality development. Through Fox Faculty, the company invests in training and developing the next generation of hospitality professionals, while Fox Vacations supports the group through inbound and outbound travel services.

Sustainability is an important part of this journey. Fox Resorts has introduced initiatives across its properties covering water conservation and wastewater reuse, solar hot water, reduced single-use plastics, responsible waste management, linen-reuse programmes and community clean-ups. The company also works with local artisans and creatives, supports community and animal welfare initiatives and has begun aligning its operations with the Global Sustainable Tourism Council (GSTC) framework.

The Capital Maharaja Group CEO Suresh Srinivasan said:  “This recognition reflects what we believe is fundamental to building strong and enduring businesses — investing in people, giving them the opportunity to grow, and creating a culture where excellence becomes a shared responsibility.” 

“Fox Resorts is a shining example of how that philosophy translates into a business that continues to strengthen its offering, develop its people and contribute meaningfully to Sri Lanka’s hospitality sector. We are very proud to see the team’s work recognised on a South Asian stage,” he added.

Capital Maharaja Group is one of Sri Lanka’s most established diversified business groups, with interests spanning media, consumer products, industrial businesses, technology, services, travel and hospitality. Its longstanding focus on people, entrepreneurship and investment in Sri Lankan enterprise continues to provide the foundation for the growth of Fox Resorts.

That growth will continue in December 2026, when Fox Resorts expands its portfolio with the opening of its new luxury wellness hotel in Kirinda, Yala. Combining an intimate beachfront setting with Ayurveda-inspired therapies, yoga, meditation, nutrition, mindfulness and curated wellness programs, the property will offer travellers to and within Sri Lanka a distinctive new wellness experience rooted in nature and Sri Lankan hospitality.

Fox Resorts CEO Chris Quyn said:  “We are immensely proud of this recognition, and particularly proud of the team that earned it. Our guests are at the heart of everything we do, and this award reflects the care, consistency and warmth our teams bring to them every day. As we expand into Yala and wellness, those same values will continue to define Fox Resorts.”

The South Asian Travel Awards, established in 2016, is one of the region’s recognised platforms for excellence in travel, tourism and hospitality, with nominees assessed through a rigorous process incorporating independent industry evaluation and public voting.

For Fox Resorts, said being named Leading Hospitality Development Company 2026 is a proud recognition of how far the company, its people and its properties have come — and a strong foundation for the next stage of its growth. “Above all, it is an achievement shared by every member of the Fox Resorts team and every guest who has been part of its journey,” Fox Resorts added.

The Hotels Association of Sri Lanka (THASL) has officially launched the Sri Lanka Tourism Excellence Awards 2026 (SLTEA 2026), a major national initiative dedicated to honoring outstanding performance, innovation, sustainability, and exceptional service across the country’s tourism and hospitality sector. 

Driven by the central theme, “Celebrating Excellence, Inspiring Innovation, and Shaping the Future of Tourism,” the awards program aims to showcase extraordinary achievements while inspiring industry-wide adherence to sustainable and responsible tourism practices.

Built upon the three pillars of Sustainability, Hospitality, and Excellence, the SLTEA 2026 acknowledges impactful contributions spanning eco-conscious initiatives, authentic guest engagement, cutting-edge digital transformation, and exemplary leadership. Participation is open to any enterprise registered with the Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority (SLTDA) that has maintained active operations in Sri Lanka for at least three years. To ensure fair competition, participating entities will be evaluated across six operational scales, ranging from Micro, Small, and Medium enterprises to Mid-Large, Large, and Extra-Large establishments.

Applications will undergo a rigorous three-tier evaluation process comprising an initial documentary assessment, comprehensive on-site verifications, and final deliberations by an independent Panel of Judges. 

Submissions will be appraised across seven core dimensions: Service Excellence; Guest Experience and Product Excellence; Innovation, Digital Transformation and Global Reach; Sustainability and Responsible Tourism; Operational, Financial and Performance Excellence; People, Leadership and Governance; and Industry, Destination and Socio-Economic Impact.

The awards ceremony, scheduled for 26 January 2027, will confer over 70 accolades, including overall Gold, Silver, and Bronze distinctions, alongside criteria-specific and sector-focused honours. Beyond the event, recipients will secure three-year usage rights to the official SLTEA emblem, permanent induction into the virtual Hall of Fame, feature coverage in leading publications, and key opportunities to share best practices across national and international industry platforms.

THASL invites all eligible hospitality and tourism organisations across Sri Lanka to submit their applications, benchmark their achievements against national standards, and join a collective movement driving the future growth and global prestige of Sri Lankan tourism.

title: Otherland Hotels makes its debut in Galle | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 22 October 2026 00:00
-     - 6

The founders (from left) Emanuel Siddhartha, Rishi Sreedharan and Samarth Gowda

DESIGNED by Studio Camarada, led by Andre Camara, Orherland Hotels has opened its first property, Otherland Galle, introducing a lifestyle hospitality concept that brings together design-led accommodation, destination dining, music and locally curated experiences on Sri Lanka’s southern coast.

Officially opened on 12 October 2026, the 66-key property is located on Matara Road, approximately 400 metres from Dewata Beach and 2.8 kilometres from Galle Fort, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Drawing on the region’s surf culture, culinary traditions and creative communities, the hotel is designed to encourage guests to explore the destination beyond conventional sightseeing.

Founded by Rishi Sreedharan, Samarth Gowda and Emanuel Siddhartha in partnership with Beryll Group, Otherland Hotels is built around the philosophy ‘Never the Same Twice’. Its approach places experiences, design and cultural discovery at the centre of hospitality, combining private rooms and suites with shared accommodation and lively communal spaces.

“Otherland Galle should feel like yours from the moment you walk in,” said Co-founder Samarth Gowda. “Luxury has often come with a sense of distance, with places appearing impressive because they do not feel accessible to everyone. That is not what we are building. Everything here is designed around who you are and how you want to spend your time.”

Designed by Studio Camarada, led by Andre Camara, the property features interconnected spaces that move away from the conventional hotel layout. Its interiors draw inspiration from the southern coast, incorporating sandy neutrals, ocean blues, earthy tones, rattan, ash, hand-tufted textiles and marble finishes.

The accommodation comprises 24 Ocean Rooms, 25 Terra Rooms, 12 suites and five dormitories, catering to couples, groups of friends, solo travellers and culturally curious visitors. Rooms range from 27 square metres to a 70-square-metre Patio Suite, with ocean-facing views and vistas across Galle’s mangroves and railway tracks. The property also includes rooms designed for guests with disabilities.

At ground level, Bar-kery serves as the hotel’s reception, coffee shop, bakery, aperitivo counter and informal co-working space. Its Vinyl Corner invites guests to browse records and select their own music, creating a more interactive approach to the traditional hotel lobby. The all-day concept offers coffee, seasonal fruit juices, tea, house-made gelato and cocktails, alongside breakfast dishes influenced by Sri Lankan and international flavours. Colombo Coffee Company has developed an exclusive signature blend for the property.

The rooftop venue, Creatures, combines a restaurant, cocktail bar, infinity pool and music space, with 270-degree views of the Indian Ocean and Galle coastline. During the day, it offers dining, swimming and sundowners before transitioning into an evening social venue featuring curated music and cocktails.

The food program, led by Chef Rajeev Kumar, draws on Sri Lankan culinary traditions while incorporating international influences and contemporary techniques. Dishes include King Coconut Ceviche, Yellowfin Tuna Tataki, Lankan Fish Cutlets and Devilled Pork Ribs glazed with kithul treacle. Desserts include a Watalappam Brûlée, reinterpreting the traditional coconut and jaggery custard.

The cocktail program is led by Arijit Bose, whose portfolio includes hospitality concepts in Bengaluru and Goa, while day-to-day operations are managed by Aneesha Thapa. Music forms an equally important part of Creatures, with a Void sound system supporting a programme of resident DJs, live performances and international artist residencies. Weekly sessions span soulful Afro music, R&B, folk, funk, jazz fusion, house, techno and electronica.

Beyond the property, guests can explore The Other Side, Otherland’s experience program developed in collaboration with local surfers, fishermen, artisans, guides, chefs and musicians. Its offerings range from curry masterclasses and guided walks through Galle Fort to surf lessons at Dewata Beach, whale-watching excursions off Mirissa and kayaking through the mangroves of Koggala Lake. Rooftop sunset sessions, arrack tastings, beach cricket and tuk-tuk bar crawls add a social dimension to the programme.

“At Otherland, curiosity is the operating principle,” said Co-founder Rishi Sreedharan. “We measure success by whether guests leave with a real sense of Galle. The surfers, fishermen, chefs and craftspeople who live here have helped build these experiences, and they are the ones bringing them to life.”

The property’s opening marks the first phase of Otherland Galle’s development, with a gym, wellness centre and banquet facilities planned as part of a subsequent phase.

title: Sri Lanka’s wildlife fascinates global stage in Belgium | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 22 October 2026 00:00

Sri Lanka Embassy in Belgium with the sponsorship of Sri Lanka Tourism Promotion Bureau organised screening of a stunning Sri Lankan wildlife documentary produced by RTBF broadcasting organisation to the Le Jardin Extraordinaire (The extraordinary garden), a premier natural & environmental documentary program of RTBF targeting the French-speaking community in Belgium. The inaugural screening took place on October 10, 2026, at Le Delta, the Provincial Cultural Centre in Namur, as part of the renowned Namur International Nature Festival. Over 400 nature enthusiasts, conservationists, and lovers of biodiversity gathered to experience the thrilled wildlife and rich fauna of Sri Lanka at the inaugural screen.

Ambassador Chandana Weerasena and the Embassy team attended the inaugural screening. Following the screening, the Ambassador participated in an interactive question-and-answer session with the renowned journalist & famous wildlife filmmaker in Belgium, Tanguy Dumortier, who joined the RTBF TV crew for filming in Sri Lanka. The discussion highlighted Sri Lanka’s exceptional natural heritage, distinctive wildlife and potential as a destination for nature-based tourism.

Sri Lanka Embassy in Belgium in collaboration with the Sri Lanka Tourism Promotion Bureau facilitated filming of this special edition of Belgian wildlife documentary Le Jardin Extraordinaire in Sri Lanka by the RTBF team in early this year with the objective of showcasing the island’s rich biodiversity, unique ecosystems, and exceptional natural beauty to the millions of viewers in Belgium and other French-speaking markets.  

The documentary team covered several of Sri Lanka’s most significant wildlife destinations, including national wildlife parks Wilpattu, Udawalawa, Kumana and the Sinharaja Rainforest. Jetwing Eco Holidays Ltd., will served as the official accommodation and travel partner for the TV crew during their stay in Sri Lanka.

Le Jardin Extraordinaire is Belgium’s longest-running television program and one of the oldest nature documentary program in European television history. First broadcast on 3 October 1965, the program recently celebrated its 60th anniversary on RTBF, the French-language public broadcaster in Belgium.

As a part of the promotional activities, Sri Lankan tourism brochures were distributed among participants, while tourism promotional banners were showcased at the venue. Ceylon tea was also served to guests, providing a further opportunity to introduce attendees to one of Sri Lanka’s internationally recognised products.

Tourist arrivals from Belgium to Sri Lanka recorded the highest-ever number in 2025, and this forthcoming wildlife documentary which will be telecasted on RTBF TV channel in November 2026 is expected to further strengthen Sri Lanka’s visibility as a premier nature and eco-tourism destination and a rich biodiversity hotspot, contributing to sustained growth in tourist arrivals from Belgium and other French-speaking regions in years to come.
